speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. That this House express its grave disappointment and great concern that the President of the United States has refused to sign the United Nations Law of the Sea Treaty.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF MICROTECHNOLOGY ON WOMEN OFFICE WORKERS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity regarding the future for female clerical workers in Canada. The recent conference, "Women and the Impact of Microtechnology", which drew together 500 participants representing community groups, concerned women, trade unions and employers from across Canada, pointed out that technological advances in the office workplace will have dramatic and adverse effects on the clerical service sector. The overwhelming majority of these workers are women, and over 40 per cent are in danger of losing their jobs to rapid microtechnological advances in the office environment. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King):
That the members of this House urge that measures be taken by employers and the government to ensure that the problem is properly defined and that appropriate training and retraining be done on a large scale to prevent massive unemployment and to ensure that these positive advancements in the office workplace do not result in adverse effects on the majority of women who work there.

This altered the one half capital cost allowance in the year of purchase for the daily car rental businesses, but left out the dealer-leasing businesses. The dealer-leasing businesses should be included, as both groups operate on the same principle, one on the day basis and the other for longer periods. speechtext:

2.	The answers in Part 1 are affected by many assumptions, a partial list of which is as follows:
1.	rates of increase in average earnings
2.	rates of increase in the Consumer Price Index
3.	rates of interest on new investments
4.	mortality rates

6.	participation rates in the plan
7.	earnings distributions
8.	retirement ages

10.	rates of emergence of spouses' pensions
11.	proportions married, age distributions, and relative
earnings distributions of husbands and wives
12.	remarriage rates of widows and widowers.
These, as well as other assumptions, are described in considerable detail in Statutory Actuarial Report No. 6.
The combined effect of all assumptions on expenditures and contributions for the three calendar years 1978 to 1980 has been that actual expenditures have averaged about 92 per cent of estimated while actual contributions have averaged about 97 per cent of estimated. The net result shows that actual experience has been somewhat more favourable than estimated, and if this trend should persist, the actual dates of occurrence of one or more of the three contingencies considered in Part 1, assuming no change in the contribution rate, may be slightly later than those estimated.
As to some specific assumptions, the annual rate of increase in average earnings, the annual rate of increase in the Consumer Price Index, and the annual rate of interest on new investments were projected to decrease from experience levels in 1978 to ultimate levels of 5.5 per cent, 3.5 per cent and 6.5 per cent respectively for 1983 and later. While these ultimate rates appear to be definitely on the low side, at least for the short-term future, it should be emphasized that the estimates in Statutory Acturial Report No. 6 are affected much more by the assumed differentials between these rates than by their absolute levels. For example, again assuming no change in the 3.6 per cent contribution rate, if ultimate assumptions of 11.5 per cent, 9.5 per cent and 12.5 per cent had been used instead (i.e., assumptions involving the same differentials but 6 percentage points higher), (a) the year when estimated expenditures would exceed contributions would still have been 1985, (b) the year when estimated expenditures would exceed contributions plus interest would have been 1995 instead of 1993, while (c) the year when the fund would cease to exist would have been 2002 instead of 2003. Evidently, these changes would have been relatively minor.

The Canadian government will implement a system for providing loans at 3 to 6 per cent below the market rate to ensure long-term security.
He then went on to say:
I stress again people who purchase new housing will do so with the confidence that they can renew their mortgages at lower than market interest rates.
Yesterday in the House of Commons the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was asked whether the Government of Canada had in fact come to a definitive conclusion with regard to the implementation of that policy, whether that policy was in effect and the Prime Minister could give assurance to those people who were advised by the minister of housing to proceed on the basis of that proposal contained in the budget to purchase a home, and whether the government through the Prime Minister was able to assure those people that that reduction in interest rates would be forthcoming.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday, in the first part of my speech, I mentioned that inflation is at the root of our problems. I also mentioned a number of disastrous effects inflation was having on our society, and 1 said that it was because of this high inflation rate that our economy was in its present state, and that 1,300,000 Canadians were out of work. I also said that we were asking the nine million Canadians who were employed to help us protect their jobs and to find work for those Canadians who are unemployed today. I also mentioned that the government was spending $2 billion per month on its income redistribution programs. I also tried to illustrate what $1 billion represents. I could explain it another way, namely, that one billion seconds ago, the Second World War ended. One billion minutes ago, Jesus Christ was on earth and one billion hours ago, man was living in caves.

I was responding, Mr. Speaker, to the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, who says he could not understand how wage cuts could help get our economy moving. In this sense, I would like to quote a portion of a Financial Post article entitled "Wage restraint does matter". I might add that this also answers the challenge that was put to us yesterday by

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn). The article states as follows:
In general, evidence of the need to moderate wage demands is all around us. Look, for example, at the U.S., our biggest customer. In the first quarter of 1982, U.S. wage settlements in the industrial sector average increases of only 2.2 per cent in the first year of contract. Excluding the teamsters and the auto workers, who accepted a wage freeze, the average increase was still an extraordinarily modest 6.8 per cent. For 1981, U.S. settlements in all sectors were about four percentage points below Canadian settlements. The U.S. federal civil service has been limited to a 4.8 per cent increase. In the face of these trends-and the wage restraint in other countries with which we must trade and compete-the reaction of Canadian labour leaders to Ottawa's proposals has been disappointing. In particular, the response so far of Canadian Labour Congress President Dennis McDermott, with personally offensive references to the Finance minister, and hints of a general strike, is a perfect example of just what we don't need.
I say to Mr. McDermott: "Do you think that by pricing ourselves out of the market through wage increases about double what they are in the United States, we are going to help our economy recover?" 1 might add that I was encouraged by the reaction of Mr. McDermott after his meeting with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and I can only hope that this will carry through to a positive reaction on his part.
The federal government in its budget is facing reality. What the federal government has done is to show strong leadership, the kind of leadership our country needs and the kind of leadership that 1 am convinced Canadians will respond to in a very positive way. I would like to suggest to the members opposite, and particularly to those in the New Democratic Party, that they forget about criticizing our approach in order to try to win votes. I would say to them: "If you really want to help your constituents, you will encourage them to join the fight against inflation and to restrict their wage demands to 6 per cent."
There are countless suggestions, Mr. Speaker, as to how to solve our economic problems. The first difficult task, of course, was to select and put forth a plan of action. Strong leadership requires this and our government is providing it. It is time now for all Canadians collectively to adopt this policy and to win this battle.
It was suggested yesterday by the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) that this bill is unfair. I would like to remind him that it is going to be unfair only if the nine million Canadians who are working today refuse to co-operate, refuse to help us find jobs for those Canadians who are out of work. The hon. member is assuming that Canadians who are working will refuse us that help. He has adopted a negative attitude.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that when I was head of Canada Steamship Lines and I had to hire people, I looked for four things: first, their knowledge; second, their skill; third, their habits; and fourth, their attitude. No matter how good their knowledge was, how perfect their skill, how good their habits, if their attitude was negative they were absolutely worthless. I might say to the member for Kootenay West that under that program I could not have hired him.
As I said at the outset of my speech last night, I think this is probably the most important piece of legislation on which this House will have to pass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Inflation has to be brought under control for the simple reason that the alternatives of more unemployment, higher interest rates and greater deficits are absolutely unthinkable.
Let me review some editorials which I think will help us make a few points. Under the headline "The Wrong Whipping boy" the Montreal Gazette of July 8 wrote the following:
There is nothing necessarily wrong with paying people a lot of money. What is wrong is to pay high wages and salaries that are not earned through increasingly efficient production. Canadian efficiency-our productivity-has been lagging dangerously behind that of competing nations.
Those hon. members who speak about our purchasing power have a tendency to forget about this principle.
On July 6 under the headline "Unemployment data should be a warning", The Globe and Mail stated:
The OECD, in a report on the Canadian economy last week, warned that Canada has poor prospects for restoring sustained and balanced economic growth as long as present trends continue-even if it turns out there is a recovery in export markets.
With a faster rate of inflation in Canada than in the United States and, contributing to the inflation problem, a markedly higher rate of increase in wage rates under collective agreements, this country is in a poor position to take advantage of any opportunities that may develop in export markets.
In the longer run, if pay increases under collective agreements do not soon move down to 6 or 7 per cent from a recent rate of about 12 per cent, Canada's job prospects must remain bleak. It would seem obvious that, if Western Europe lacks confidence in its ability to compete against Japan and the United States in high technology products and against Japan and the newly industrialized nations in labour intensive goods, then Canada has even more reason to worry.
Mr. Leo De Bever, who is a director for Chase Econometrics, was interviewed on the CBC as follows:
Is the 6 per cent solution in fact a solution to this sort of thing?
Mr. De Bever answered:
Well, I think so. Obviously, the key element in this budget that would make a lot of difference ... would be if the private sector were to agree with what the finance minister is asking for. The likelihood of that happening is obviously very small. I think there are a lot of people in this economy who would be willing to do what the finance minister says if they were assured that, say, 75 or 80 per cent of the population were in the same boat.
The second question by the CBC was the following:
You mean workers would be willing to accept that sort of thing?
The following is the answer:
I think so. I don't think anybody advocating large wage gains at this point is a friend of labour because ultimately those gains are going to be eroded. It would be much better if we all throttled back, if we all decided look, enough is enough. Let's just forget about making short-term gains. Let's just take that 5 per cent cut in standard of living that we would be accepting if we were going to go to 6 per cent. And let's get it over with. Let's get back on the track that is sustainable.
An article in the Montreal Gazette of June 29 by Hugh Anderson entitled "After three tries. MacEachen finally rates a pass" states:
July 13, 1982

The government plans to control what it has direct power over (its own employees' pay cheques), to influence pay and prices where it can do so indirectly (telephone bills and farm-product prices, for instance) and persuade or shame the rest of us into line.
There is even the promise that the pay of cabinet ministers, members of parliament and senators will actually be cut. That might make the whole thing popular enough to succeed.
I certainly hope so. Under the headline "Six per cent or bust", The Vancouver Sun of June 30 stated:
The proposed 6 per cent limit on public-service pay increases (to drop to 5 per cent next year) was essential. The provinces have to go along with it as well as with similar limits on cost increases for public services. Those in greatest need will get inflation-indexed assistance but everyone else will be fairly limited to 6 per cent increases in benefits.
But Mr. MacEachen has appealed only for voluntary controls in the private sector. Will Canadians respond? They should, but the battles this summer between labour and employers will probably be fierce and costly.
If the incomes policy works it will bring down inflation. Mr. MacEachen said the government will not budge from its tight monetary policy, which will also help in reducing inflation.
The final editorial is from the Regina Leader-Post and is entitled "New budget offers us chance to bind rather than bicker". It states:
The pay measure is a restriction of 6 per cent on federal salaries this year and 5 per cent next year. The opposition's quick support for this move was encouraging, for it suggests that the Conservatives intend to help, rather than impede, solution of the national crisis before it can become an economic disaster. That does not mean that there is not room for the opposition parties to make suggestions to fine-tune MacEachen's budget proposals. But with Canada facing the need to mobilize economically, this is the time for what the Americans call a bipartisan approach-make that tripartisan, if the NDP agrees-to provide expeditious passage of effective economic remedies.
I think we are entering a period of our history in which we have to fight for our lives. We have to fight to save this country, which will go down the drain economically unless we do something, I think we have to forget our bipartisanship. We have to get together. We cannot afford to lose this battle. 1 implore all Canadians wherever they may be to do their bit to help cure our economic ailments so that Canada can remain the best country in the world, which it is today.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a good deal of pleasure, albeit very anxious pleasure, to speak in this debate on Bill C-124 entitled the "Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act", a bill which provides legislative authority for public sector compensation restraint, the so-called six and five rule announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his budget speech on June 28. The bill would also restrict-in fact cut-the salaries of Members of Parliament and senators for the balance of the present fiscal year. Surprisingly, the bill also includes within its framework a provision which effectively eliminates the right of public servants in Canada to strike upon the expiry of their present collective agreements.
I noted with interest the remarks of the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Desmarais) who was partially correct in identifying the problem as inflation. He suggested that we must all form part of a positive initiative to reduce the toll that inflation is taking of society as a result of the devastating effects of unemployment, increasing business bankruptcies and related factors. Although the hon. member said the problem is caused
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
by inflation, he did not point out where inflation originates. I should like to point out to him that it is not wage earners or workers or taxpayers who cause inflation; it is governments that create inflation and it is governments that have the power to reduce or eliminate it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who interrupts knows very well that it is governments that overprint the money supply in advance of election campaigns in order to be able to give away various goodies and gimmicks in an effort to coerce and mislead the voter. It is governments that subsequently raise taxes in a malicious and devious way, in total violation of their election promises.
I might single out this government in particular. It said it was going to hold the increase in the excise tax on gasoline to less than 14 cents per gallon. It is governments that allow the continuation of high interest rates, that borrow heavily and incur massive deficits to the extent that the financial requirements of the private sector cannot be raised. It is governments that create more and more Crown corporations and more and more means of intervention to frustrate, restrain and ultimately eliminate the private, competitive economy.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Dollard has left the chamber, Mr. Speaker. I think he should realize that if we in opposition sometimes appear negative-after all, it is our role to provide constructive criticism-it is because we do not always agree with the initiatives the government is taking. We most particularly do not agree with the suggestion that there is only one way to solve the problems confronting our economy and that that is the way of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance. Apparently it is to be six and five or we all go down together, and then we will be faced with controls, as the Prime Minister has threatened.
The suggestion of the hon. member for Dollard that anyone who speaks against the government's legislative program is taking a negative and pessimistic view is repulsive to members of the opposition. Some of us may feel that certain initiatives in Bill C-124 and in the budget are positive and good for the country. Yet, we are entitled to stand in this House and speak negatively or creatively to use a better word, about measures proposed by the government or about the lack of measures that we believe should be taken to deal with the current economic plight of the country. We agree that inflation is a serious problem for Canadians and that negative attitudes are bad. Incompetent leadership is worse, however, and that is what has brought this country to its economic knees.
The measures contained in Bill C-124 which would ensure that salary demands within the public service are limited to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year are, I believe, a small step in the right direction. They are certainly not fair and equitable in that they show no selectivity in terms of eliminating the wasteful practices of the government; nonetheless, they are a small step in the right direction. However, they

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
assume that every clerk, every employee, every deputy minister who receives this 6 per cent restriction is equally important to the goals of our nation and that, rather than eliminate the waste and inefficiency that exist in government, we should all equally pay the price. Although this is a small step in the right direction, it avoids the crucial and central reasons for our economic dilemma.
It is all well and good to bring in the 6 per cent and 5 per cent limits which in the projections for the fiscal year 1982-83 will save the government some $500 million, or an average of $1,000 for every public servant. Yet, in itself, $500 million is a very small amount when compared to the gross national product of the country which, even in a state of decline, is $300 billion. Because of the policies of the government and its inability to manage the economy, a 2 per cent decline in the gross national product is predicted for the coming fiscal year. That means a $6 billion decline in our net economic output. Will that be overcome by restraining increases in public service salaries by $500 million? The serious structural problems in our economy will cost the country over $6 billion in lost potential, just to maintain the same gross national product as last year. That is 12 times the savings in salaries expected as a result of this bill.
This bill and its parent, the budget of June 28, does not come to grips with the problem of a $6 billion decline in the gross national product. Even if the bill might be seen as a small step in the right direction, the savings will amount to but a pittance. It will not help us or the health of our ailing economy, nor create the jobs that are so desperately needed. Furthermore, it will not ensure that there will be equity for public service employees. Some people may be entitled to an increase higher than 6 per cent, but there are others whose salaries could justifiably be cut, including cabinet ministers whose salaries, I submit, should be cut to $1.
The budget of June 28 is based on economic intervention and redistribution of income by actions of the federal government. Instead of creating new wealth for all and placing emphasis on productive economics and finding ways to unburden the private sector, it is based upon redistribution, upon pessimism and upon a lowering of our expectations. This is the most bountiful nation in the world but we are not realizing our potential.
Many commentators on the budget, including the well-known columnist Mr. Don McGillivray, have said that we will not solve the problems of the economy by raising taxes once again. In spite of the $20 billion deficit and the dangerous implications of this for the country, we cannot continue to expect to raise taxes as a means of pulling Canada out of this difficult dilemma. Taxes are only a measure of the production of the country. If productivity is not increased, if the gross national product is not increased, if the return on an hour's labour is not increased, then we have no hope of solving our economic problems.
If we cannot encourage people to work harder and engage in more entrepreneurial enterprises, the gross national product and the tax flow to government will not be increased. The budget of November 12 increased taxes massively by $10
billion to $12 billion through several concealed devices. Through its deindexing provisions, the budget of June 28 raised the taxes paid by an average couple with two children and an income of roughly $25,000 per year by $1,000 over and above any inflationary increment.
Once again the government, which should have realized the errors of its ways from the damage caused by the budget of November 12, has brought in another budget which raises taxes. In raising taxes by more than the inflationary increment, it has the gall to tell Canadians, particularly public servants, that their incomes have to be restrained to something less than the inflationary increment. There is something seriously wrong, Mr. Speaker, in a government which approaches the problems of this nation in that way. This program, and the budget which encompasses it, creates more work for bureaucrats, creates more programs, and expands the centre of gravity here in Ottawa. To you, Mr. Speaker, that may be a welcome initiative, but to many of us representing other parts of Canada it is at the heart of our national dilemma.
The budget shows no understanding of the remedies needed for the fundamental structural problems plaguing our industrial and primary resource sectors. The government is preoccupied with cutting 5 per cent or 6 per cent from government payrolls and creating a bunch of new programs which will keep a lot more bureaucrats running around like squirrels, receiving applications, judging them, weighing them and comparing them with income tax records and StatsCan statistics. Then, after a panel sits in judgment on every application, perhaps there will be a decision made. All that does is delay things, Mr. Speaker, and add to the inefficiency of this government.
There is no mention, Mr. Speaker, in these current economic initiatives of the collapse of Alsands and what might have caused it. They do not mention that we would have had 30,000 more jobs in this country today had the Minister of Finance opposite and his NDP colleagues not brought down the Clark government in December, 1979. There is no mention of the cancellation of the Cold Lake project and the Alaska gas pipeline, or the decline of our manufacturing industries and productivity as measured by every index, as has been cited over and over again in this House.
We in this party, Mr. Speaker, want to see a positive attitude restored to Canadians. We want to see confidence restored in the decisions which affect the development of our economy. But we cannot see that happening as long as the government persists in wrong-headed initiatives. These show how incompetent the government is. It is unable to understand that our economy was built and is based on, and has thrived for more than a century because of, the business and private sectors.
I for one, Mr. Speaker, would be happy to stand up in this House and commend the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, or anyone else who would get up and say yes, maybe we made a few mistakes. Maybe some opposition members have been saying the right things for the last two years. Maybe
July 13, 1982

they are not all just a bunch of screaming radicals from Newfoundland, western Canada or the western Arctic. Maybe they do know something about the way the people out there feel about the values, initiatives and talents which can be brought to bear in resolving our national economic dilemma. But, Mr. Speaker, we do not hear that from members opposite. We certainly do not hear it from the Prime Minister, who admonishes us for not getting on to the six and five bandwagon. Well, I for one will be part of that bandwagon inasmuch as most Members of Parliament feel they are worth every dollar they earn around this place. But I would be much happier about it if this government had the competence and the courtesy to recognize that other people know something about economics and the dilemma that faces our nation.
We should be taking positive export-oriented initiatives, Mr. Speaker, instead of finding more gimmicky programs to redistribute the existing and ever-diminishing pool of wealth. The population is not diminishing, so why are we taking a protectionist position in terms of world economics and trade? Why are we cutting ourselves off from world markets while at the same time borrowing ourselves ever further into debt and obligations to lenders in the U.S. and elsewhere? If we are to believe, as the Prime Minister tells us, that all industrialized nations are in trouble, who are these lenders who are doing so well? Who is profiting because of our ignorance, Mr. Speaker?
I think many of us in this Elouse know.
A country, just like an individual, must produce more than it consumes if it is ever to support growth, prosperity and an optimistic outlook on the future. The country must produce more than it consumes and earn more than it spends, and that means we just cannot isolate ourselves from the world, as this government will eventually lead us to do when it brings in foreign exchange controls with the support of the NDP. We cannot afford to take that kind of small-minded outlook when we have more resources per capital than any other nation in the world. We have more natural and human talents than any other country in the world, but we are frittering them away because of an incompetent understanding of the way the country works.
The deficit is of severe concern to every Canadian, Mr. Speaker. When I was home shortly after the finance minister brought in his budgetary statement and announced that next year the deficit would be up from $10 billion to $20 billion, every person who approached me said: "$20 billion! They must be out of their minds. Our kids are going to have to pay for that. If we are spending that money to stimulate growth for a successful economy, why is it not developing that way? There must be something wrong in Ottawa."
The second thing they told me, Mr. Speaker, was to go back to Ottawa and find a way, one way or another, to get rid of the government. Members opposite know that because once in a while they do go home to their ridings. They know that every one of their seats is in a very precarious position at this point, along with their indexed pensions and everything else. They know that as soon as the people get the chance they are going to throw them out. If they cannot do it by parliamentary
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
means, Mr. Speaker-and this frightens me-they may resort to other tactics. It frightens me because of the implications for my family, my friends and my community. I see signs of violence in the initiatives reflected in Bill C-124 which, in order to avert a labour shutdown in the public service, brings in a measure which abolishes the right to strike. That is the measure of the government's lack of confidence in its ability to convince Canadians of the rightness of its policies.
If the government is so right, why can it not convince the people of Canada? The best way to do that would be to call a general election and let the people decide. Oh, hon. members laugh! They know what the consequences would be. They know that three-quarters of them would lose their seats. If the people were allowed to be the judge, they would throw them all out.

speechtext: So simple.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member had been listening he would realize the problem is not so simple.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: You are so simple.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
It is not as simple as six and five. It has a lot to do with the fundamental mismanagement of our economy and a misunderstanding of the structural problems which are at the heart of our national economic dilemma.
There has been no clear-cut evidence, Mr. Speaker, in this budget, the previous budget, or in anything else this Prime Minister has done, that he cares about improving the efficiency of government or exercising restraint. It is absolutely unfair for the Government of Canada to ask people, starting with the public service, to restrain their salary expectations and then bring down a budget which has increased government spending 22 per cent over the last budget; to increase taxes far in excess of the rate of inflation, thereby contributing to inflation; or to allow interest rates to run out of control without any positive initiatives except a gimmicky program to hand back $3,000. There are no positive initiatives to eliminate waste in government or make senior public servants accountable. There is no attempt to eliminate the God-awful, foolish and extravagant throw-away programs that this government is so guilty of. I do not need to enumerate the whole list but I do want to give a few examples of why it is that in the future of this country Grit times will be known as hard times.
First is the metric promotion. Already over $60 million has been spent unnecessarily. If we had a healthy, buoyant, expanding economy, maybe we could afford that. But in addition to the $60 million spent on promotion, advertisement, brainwashing and brain-twisting people to accept the government's unwise initiatives, the businesses of Canada have had to incur major expenses to buy new scales and to convert their units of measurement. These businesses have had to go outside of Canada to obtain them because we do not supply the means to do that. It might be great for trade with France, Holland and West Germany, but it does not do Canada one bit of good.

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
That is the kind of foolish, extravagant and incompetent decision that is at the heart of our national dilemma.
Over $100 million has been spent in government advertising. Almost $1 million a day has been spent plastering our countryside with slogans like "A new Constitution for Canada"; "Working together", and so on. All of that garbage does not turn people on when they see interest rates out of sight and unemployment such that every person knows two or three friends or neighbours who are faced with that spectre.
Next is funding, and guarantees which must be purchased to buy insurance for loans to communist countries. Why are we doing that through the Export Development Corporation and other initiatives? I for one believe we should be encouraging far more trade. But if, for example, we extend an EDC guaranteed loan to build a new copper mine in Bolivia, I want to know what the benefits are to our Canadian engineering consulting community and how many dump trucks will be ordered from the United States and elsewhere to their specification in relation to the salaries generated in Canada. I want to know the impact of that on the world competitive situation. I want to know to what extent we are hamstringing our mining industry by encouraging our consultants with low-interest government guaranteed loans to go and do business and build new mining ventures in other parts of the world.
We are arguing vigorously at the United Nations through the Law of the Sea that we want to ensure adequate controls so that Canada's nickel mining industry is not adversely impacted by the drive to get on with seabed mining. We want to protect our Canadian mining industry, but while doing that, we are going about assisting and encouraging Canadian companies who want to open new mines in Bolivia, South America, Central Africa or wherever. I am in favour of that if someone would put the sums down on a piece of paper and come clean with the people of Canada, telling them how many jobs will be lost in return for the few hundreds of thousands of dollars in revenue earned by consulting firms.
There is something that has bothered me for a long time, and I am glad to see that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is in the House because the matter concerns her jurisdiction. 1 have a large family. I do not need to mention how many children I have, but my wife and I need the income we enjoy and we have always benefited by the family allowance. But I cannot understand why the government has not had the political courage to streamline the program of child tax benefits and spousal taxation on income received from family allowances. My wife receives family allowance cheques every month because we have children. I pay income tax on those moneys and then I have to declare child exemptions on my income tax. My wife has to file an application for child tax credits, which means filling out an income tax return.
That involves several different offices, several different bureaucrats, several different addresses and several pieces of paper. This costs the people of Canada an unnecessarily large amount of money. It is absolutely ridiculous that this government has not had the political courage to sort that situation out. It could be done by one annual tax credit payable to one
or other spouse. This would not proliferate and multiply the number of income tax returns for wives or husbands who do not work. But why did we encourage the virtual doubling-at least a 30 per cent increase-in the filling of income tax returns in the way the child tax credit was implemented?
It would have been far better if this government had had the smarts, the intelligence and the political will to rearrange the whole system so that one taxpayer could file for a tax credit for his or her children. You could get rid of the family allowance system, if necessary, which could be replaced with the equivalent or increased benefits to the parents of families. This could well be afforded because a huge amount of waste could be eliminated. We have taxpayers' money not going to the good of those who need it; it is going to support government bureaucrats who have a summer cottage in the Gatineau and a winter home in Florida. These people have indexed pensions and are anxious as heck to pass the age of 55 so they can retire early and go down to Florida in the winter and live in their cottage in the summer. That is where that money is going, instead of going to the parents, the children, the handicapped, the old age pensioners, the widows and the war veterans who are the ones who should be getting it.
This government lacks the political courage to restructure our whole social welfare system. This government should get rid of waste and inefficiency. This government does not have the courage to do that. I know members on all sides who are a little skeptical about family allowance. I do not say abolish it; I say supplement it. But let us extend it in a way that eliminates all the unnecessary waste and overlap in the present system. This government does not have the resolve to do that.
1 am talking about real measures of restraint which would have a substantial impact on the budgetary deficit of this country, not about $500 million cut by restraining public servants universally to a 6 per cent salary increase. They will still be able to look forward to having homes in Florida, their winter and summer trips. But that does not solve the problem of the guys in my riding whose businesses are collapsing. Nor does it solve the problems of those people in Port Alberni who do not have jobs in the pulp mill, or those unemployed in the mining industry in Labrador, Sudbury and Trail. Their jobs are gone for the summer and probably until next winter. This does not solve their problems one iota. Where are the guts, the political courage, that could bring about a real solution to this disastrous situation in Canada?
Canada is going to build a new embassy in Washington. That might be great. It is like the desire to have a new airport terminal that many people would like to see here in Ottawa. That may be desirable, but why do we not solve our economic problems first? Why is that embassy not put on hold? Why do we not send Arthur Erickson back to Vancouver? Pay him off if we have to, but stop the embassy, Mr. Speaker.
1 know what I am going to speak about next is a little sensitive here in Ottawa, but I understand the Prime Minister has promised $500 million to $800 million to build a new art gallery and a new national museum here. I like to entertain
July 13, 1982

people in Ottawa. It is the greatest city in the world other than Vancouver, and Richmond, from where 1 come. There are a lot of museums to see in Ottawa. People who come here have an awfully good time. Maybe they need something to look forward to in ten years' time when they come back. But right now this country cannot afford a national art gallery and a new museum when people out in my part of the country are hungry and are losing their homes.
Where is the courage to eliminate or delay those decisions? The government knows that it cannot delay these things because its members know they will not be in office for a long time after the next election. This government is playing for votes with the arts and the cultural community in this country, and that is wrong.
Next let me mention travel allowances for government employees and members. We all enjoy 52 trips a year. I think it is important that members be allowed to go home to their ridings. If you wanted to cut out some of the wasteful government spending, Mr. Speaker, maybe you could save a lot more than is being saved by restraining salaries by reducing the frequency of members' trips to their ridings. I think the Canadian people would understand that, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian people expect us to be here in Ottawa sorting out this horrendous problem. It is not just the $20 billion debt this year which means that every Canadian citizen has another $1,000 debt in their pocket. It is another $4,000 per capita because the gross public debt of the Government of Canada is $100 billion.
Why does this government not continue to sit in Ottawa? We do not have to go home quite as often. We still have our telephone privileges. We still have radio, television and newspapers. Why do we not take some of those kinds of initiatives I have mentioned? Where is the positive enthusiasm on the other side for them? I think some Liberal members would be happier staying in Ottawa these days than going home.
What about travel allowances for deputy ministers and senior bureaucrats who flit around the world? These have been mentioned by some of my colleagues. These people stay only at the best places and eat the best meals, and they travel first class if they are above a certain rank. Where are the guts to resolve that kind of waste?
I have another small example. The post office in Vancouver has had a customer service office for many years where people went in to get help with their mail. Gosh knows, they needed a lot of help! Now they have some ambitious young person with a cushy government position; she is friendly with the-well, I will not say more. But for some reason the customer service area in the Vancouver post office is undergoing a major transformation. Over $150,000 will be spent on new draperies and carpets to change that area into an employment centre.
People need to be employed in the country but not by the post office. We are told that the volume of mail has diminished considerably since the 30-cent stamp was introduced. We are now hearing, as we did in the House today, that the stamp price might be increased to 33 cents or 35 cents, but probably
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
in excess of 6 per cent. This is so that they can have new draperies, and carpets to boot, in the new employment centre in the Vancouver post office. Whoever made that foolish decision ought to be fired. Canadians cannot afford such extravagance at a time when there are hungry, hurting and unemployed people across the country.
Now let me turn to the area of government printing. I am fully sympathetic to the objectives and the implementation of the Official Languages Act. I think we could print every government document in both official languages and serve the needs of all Canadians in all parts of the country by having those documents available in either English or French. For the life of me, I cannot understand why we publish everything in both official languages in one volume, as in the case of documents which members receive in their offices. Usually they are back to front and we have to flip them upside down or turn them around.
I would be happier to pick the English or French version off the rack. This wastes high quality, polished Canadian bond paper which is an export product. We are burning it. Half the pages in everything we receive are read, and I doubt whether members even read 10 per cent of what they receive. Half of those pages are wasted; they are absolutely unnecessary. I have many constituents who have now adopted the practice of sending those documents back to me to send on to the minister. These are elected officials in my own riding. They cannot stand the sight of that absolutely unnecessary waste.
When we have the printing press and the typeset to print in either English or French, we could make documents half as thick. We could print many less copies because we would need approximately half as many copies to serve the same number of people. This is just another example of the foolish extravagance which the government does not have the courage or intelligence to confront.	,
Turning to the area of new cars for cabinet ministers, let me indicate that they ride around pretty comfortably. 1 do not envy them; I know they have many pressures on them and their lives, but why do they need new cars every year? Why are we not exporting cars? If we were building cars for export, we would not become involved in the type of mess in which we became involved with Iraq. We should really build cars for export the way the Japanese do; but no, we build cars for cabinet ministers because taxpayers like to see them ride around in comfort and style! Why does the government not cut the budget for the motor car allowances of ministers? I did not see such a provision in either of the last two budgets.
When I drive around Ottawa at night I see those glorious buildings across the river in Hull all lit up. All the lights are on, and there are probably a few on Parliament Hill as well. Why? Some people will say that hydro power is cheap and that Quebec provides it, but the Government of Canada and ultimately the people pay the bill for all those lights. We have a crisis in the country but the burning of lights and the setting off of fireworks does not give a stranger visiting the country any notion that we have a serious financial problem. However,

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
we know we have a problem and the government ought to have the courage to rectify that situation by turning out the lights every night. Some people say that those lights are on time clocks. Well, where the heck are the people who used to pull the switches? That is the problem; everything is on a time clock and no one really puts oneself out to help the country out of its national dilemma. Ultimately and finally that charge has to be registered with hon. members opposite, because they have the power of the vote in the Elouse and the authority to make such changes, but they do not have the political will to do so.
Why are we purchasing new Challenger jets for cabinet ministers to flit around the country with their friends? I rode in one of those a time or two and I noticed there were often quite a few ministerial aides and others riding along. They were treated pretty well. Now we will have more ministerial aides, more deputy ministers, more senators and others flying around in nice new Challenger jets. They were supposed to have been a product to make money for Canada. Let us export them, if they are any good at all, and make money for Canadians.
I was offended about a week or so after the new Constitution was proclaimed to see a man come down the hall outside my office and unload huge packages of junk; a nice fancy display kit which someone, who obtained the government contract, prepared to display all the fancy paraphernalia and printed material to proclaim the grandeur of the great constitutional coup of the Prime Minister. Why are Canadians being asked to pay for that and all other paraphernalia which we can ill afford at this particular time in our history?
Also there are flags and the pins. I like to give people little lapel pins, as we all do, at parades and on sports days, but right now we cannot afford them. It does not make a cent for Canadians. I am concerned about national pride, but I think Canadians would be more proud of their country if it were economically healthy and people were working. I do not think we need those fancy little desk flags with screw-in bases which are all packaged up in nice red and white boxes, most of which contain hot air. They are shipped out in rail cars to western Canada, for example to my constituency office. They are shipped in huge boxes which take up three-quarters of my office space. Why were those flags not neatly rolled up around little round sticks, with the bases in plastic bags, and shipped out that way? The reason is that the incompetent government has no understanding of value and value for money; it decreed that they should go out in those nice little red and white cardboard boxes. By the way, we do not need the boxes. They are manufactured from a lot of nice Canadian newsprint, pulp and paper from my province, which is being thrown away foolishly.
There are countless examples of waste in which the government could save money. We do not need bilingual games and records to encourage physical fitness, nor do we need maps issued by the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) at a time when we are faced with a serious economic dilemma. Of course, all these things are given away free.
I know I have to support this bill because we all have to show the resolve to bring about restraint, but I have only indicated one aspect of a much more severe problem. It might save the government $500 million. It does not make a dent in the $20 billion deficit, and it does not do anything about the $6 billion decline in our gross national product year over year from last year. Fundamentally I am irritated the most when government members stand and claim with such hypocrisy in the House that anyone who does not go along with them is negative, paranoid and pessimistic. I would be prepared to accept those allegations being part of the problem if hon. members opposite would also stand up and admit that they are part of the problem.
We have had the November budget of the Minister of Finance, the National Energy Program and 500 Crown corporations. These things are all part of the national problem. Also there is the foolish, extravagant waste on many unnecessary frills at this very grave time in our national history. These are really at the heart of our national dilemma.
I expect the government to take the lead. I hear it will raise the parking fees at Vancouver International Airport by 50 per cent this year. I think that would be foolish. I expect the price at Petro-Canada pumps will rise far in excess of the rate of inflation; I think that is wrong. Government must show its commitment to restraint.
I will resume my seat momentarily, but is it fair to ask public service employees and the workers of Canada to exercise restraint while the government allows continual increases in personal income taxes which destabilize and contribute negatively to our economic growth? It allows increases in income tax, in energy taxes, in interest rates and in user charges for government services. This cannot go on.
In conclusion, I must say that if the government does not wake up and listen to the message from Canadians, if the government does not stop painting everyone else as villains but looks at itself in the mirror, the people of Canada will rise up and throw the Liberal Party out of office for so long that we will not know what was the Liberal Party.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-124 is the most immoral and divisive bill which I have witnessed since being elected to the House in 1979. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) presented what he called a solidarity budget. Bill C-124 is the reverse of solidarity. This bill will victimize one group of workers in Canada, those in the public service, by imposing wage controls, by prohibiting collective bargaining, by denying the right to strike as last resort, and by denying constitutional rights to women workers.
The misnamed solidarity budget cut back cost of living increases for pensioners, and for families receiving family allowances. Under Bill C-124, the government will bring in wage controls and cut back wage increases to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year for public service employees. Of
July 13, 1982

course, as we know, the budget did nothing to control profits or to control prices. It offered no economic policies to deal with the causes of inflation or to increase consumerism, productivity and permanent jobs, not just temporary, make-work kinds of projects.
Bill C-124 mocks the very principle of solidarity as people know it in the honoured labour movement. The only solidarity that exists, as far as I can see, is the solidarity between the Tories and the Liberals, all of whom are in favour of wage controls. We will fight this bill just as long as possible. We will continue to oppose it in co-operation with the labour movement in Canada.
My colleagues have covered many of the general criticisms we have concerning Bill C-124. In the time allotted to me, I would like to summarize some of these points and then concentrate primarily on Bill C-124 as it affects women workers in the public sector and, of course, as it affects women workers across Canada.
There are a number of myths which the government and its allies in the private sector have promoted concerning workers' wages and public servants. First of all, Bill C-124 is based on the false premise that controlling wages will reduce inflation. This point was proven to be fallacious in the past. Wage controls under the Anti-Inflation Board did not reduce inflation. During the four years of wage controls, wages were reduced from 20 per cent to 7 per cent while inflation went down only about 1 per cent during that four-year period. This proves that controlling wages will not have a significant impact on inflation, yet the government for some strange reason is determined to play games on the backs of public service employees.
Second, the government introduced no policies to counteract the causes of inflation, no industrial strategy, no price controls, no controls on profits and no reduction of interest rates. This is the main inflationary policy which makes it so difficult for workers to survive. Instead, the government has once again used workers as scapegoats. As a build-up to this situation, both the Liberals and the Tories, as well as the capitalists in our society, have been promoting political propaganda. There has been a deliberate campaign to mislead the public, to encourage people to think that wage controls are a solution and that it is the civil servants who cause inflation.
The worst aspect of Bill C-124 is that it takes away collective bargaining rights, bargaining rights which we were assured by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), I might say, would be retained and guaranteed under the Constitution. Since he is here today, I would like to refer him back to the proceedings of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution, issue 43, page 69, wherein the Solicitor General stated:
Our position on the suggestion that there be a specific reference to freedom to organize and bargain collectively is that it is already covered in the freedom of association that is provided already in the declaration or in the charter.
The Solicitor General was apparently on weak ground since his own government is now ignoring the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the freedom of association provision. In effect, it
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
is taking away all collective bargaining rights from public servants for a period of at least two years.
Another myth which has been promoted is that public service wage increases are higher than those in the private sector. Here again, the facts show that public service wages have consistently been lower than those in the private sector. In 1978, private sector wages increased by 7.7 per cent while public service wages increased by only 6.7 per cent. During the first quarter of this year, private sector wages increased by 12.3 per cent and public service wages increased by 11.5 per cent. Public service wages, then, have lagged behind those in the private sector, yet this is the sector which the government has chosen for wage controls. Of course, these wage controls in the public sector are just the first target, which the government hopes will be expanded to include all Canadian workers.
The fifth myth is that wage increases have been higher than inflation. Here again, if we look at the facts we learn that not once has the percentage of wage increases in the public service been equal to the consumer price index. It is, then, apparent that wage increases, which have been won only after very hard bargaining on the part of public service unions, have been a response to inflation. They have not been the cause of it. They have been a method by which public service workers and workers throughout the country have tried to survive so that they could raise their families, pay for their groceries and live in times when the cost of living is so high. As I said earlier, the government must get at the causes rather than penalizing the victims of inflation. But of course, we know from history that it will not do it.
Finally, Bill C-124 is a bullying bill, brought in by a bullying government. The government has picked on pensioners and families in its budget, and now it is picking on workers under Bill C-124. This comes at the very time, of course, when negotiations in the public service sector are crucial, because the next two years will be the years when high technological change will be greatly increased and the impact on public employees will be very great, particularly on women employees. Instead of analysing the causes and developing positive solutions, the government again projects the blame on a scapegoat. I want to point out that psychiatrists describe this kind of sickness as a "projection mechanism", putting the blame on someone else instead of facing and trying to solve one's own problems. Therefore, it is typical of the government, a sick government, to use a sick syndrome, typical of a very sick situation which it has created itself and with which it cannot cope.
I now want to focus on Bill C-124 as it affects women workers in the public service in particular. We believe that the hardest impact will be felt by women because they are the lowest wage earners in the public service. On July 6 I questioned the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) in the House, stating that the lowest wage earners are women and that they will therefore be the hardest hit by the government's wage controls. Many single parents need increases in order to put food on the table. As hon. members will recall, the minister

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
responded by saying: "Our intention is to bring inflation down to 6 per cent"-he was quoting the Prime Minister-"in which case no one will suffer."
Well, is that not a nice platitude? We all know that he is dreaming because past experience shows that wage controls will not have any appreciable impact on inflation. Therefore, workers, particularly women workers with very low rates of pay, will receive an increase of 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year. Women workers in the public service who are ghettoized in the lowest paid secretarial and service-type jobs will have their wage increases slashed by about 50 per cent over the next year. A Public Service Commission report entitled "Women in the Canadian Public Service, 1980", states that, compared to the total population in the public service, women are unrepresented in all occupational categories except the administrative support group, a category in which the lowest paid occupations are found. This means that 70 per cent of public service jobs paying $10,000 and under are held by women. Some of these female public servants earn under $5 an hour. Many of them are trying to raise a family on their own. Either there is no other wage earner in the household, or perhaps the other partner is unemployed. Therefore, they are living at the poverty level. These are employees of the people of Canada. These are the workers whom the government, through this bill, will cut back even further with wage increases of 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent the year after.
Let us look at some of the figures. Of approximately 268,000 public servants, 35.6 per cent are women. Sixty per cent of those women workers are in teaching, nursing, clerical and secretarial occupations, hardly the kind of occupation that pays a luxury salary. Women represent 54 per cent of employees earning under $18,000. Only 12.4 per cent of all employees earn over $22,000. Most women workers earn far below the average income in the public service.
I now want to talk about the clerks. There are 50,000 clerks in the public service. Most are women employees. Many face job loss as a result of technological change. The average wage for a typist last year was $11,000. Many of these are single parents trying to raise a family on their own. They face increasingly high costs.
The situation is similar in the provincial public sector. I recently read an article about a male clerk in the province of Quebec who, after calculating his income and family costs, said that he would have more take-home pay if he were on welfare compared to his wages in the provincial public service. Last night the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) gave a number of examples of women he had talked to in skilled, service-oriented jobs who are in desperate financial straits. Let us not kid ourselves: we are not talking about high-priced executives, Members of Parliament and judges when we talk of the impact of this bill. We are talking about 50,000 female clerks who simply cannot stretch their pay cheques. It is a myth that the majority of public servants are overpaid.
I now want to deal with what has happened to clerks in recent years. In 1980 the CRs in the public service, mostly female clerks, organized and negotiated. After not having been able to negotiate wage increases that they desperately needed and deserved, for the first time in their history they went on strike for better wages. It was a first. It took a hell of a lot of guts for women workers who had no experience with that kind of activity. They picketed for several weeks, negotiated and eventually won.
That was not easy. It is not easy for workers at the low end of the pay scale, who are insecure about their jobs and have families to support, to go out on strike. That was the last thing they wanted to do. Finally, they realized it was the only way they were going to be recognized in order to negotiate for salaries that would begin to bring them up to the levels they deserved. I congratulate those public service workers and their brothers and sisters in the labour movement who supported them.
As a result of that strike action, public service clerical workers won a 16 per cent settlement, bringing some of their salaries to $10,000 or $11,000. However, that settlement was for last year. This year they are due for a 12.5 per cent settlement. It was promised to them by Treasury Board, with the President of the Treasury Board kicking and screaming all the way to the bank. The same man who is bringing in this bill has consistently opposed progressive policies that would benefit female employees.
What will happen now? Their employer, the head of the Treasury Board, has betrayed them. They bargained in good faith and won. Under Bill C-124, these rights and promises will be taken away from them. Instead of the 12.5 per cent raise which was negotiated and which they were promised for next fall, they will get only 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent the year after. They are going backward instead of forward in that category of jobs where workers are grossly underpaid.
Bill C-124 is an outright attack by the Liberal government on labour, especially low-paid women workers. It is a deliberate attack on these 50,000 clerks who fought so hard to get a decent wage. It is a union-breaking tactic that this government is bringing in designed to undermine organized labour, collective bargaining and the right to strike, which is so essential as a last resort, as I illustrated, for workers such as these female clerks. Those rights are gone for two years.
Coming back to the cost of living, we hear the argument that costs will be down to 6 per cent and everything will be rosy. Workers will get a 6 per cent increase next fall. They will be able to cover everything as though there was no change or reduction in their pay increase. I wonder how many Liberals have gone shopping lately. I wonder how many are paying off mortgages. Today we heard the minister responsible for Canada Housing and Mortgage Corporation again trying to present his wishful thinking as government policy. We know that mortgage renewals are costing many workers 65 per cent of their wages, especially those with a one-year renewal contract. The last policy brought in gives no benefit to these workers.
July 13, 1982

Rents are going up. I will be very surprised if anything is done to reduce them by next fall. When a woman goes to the grocery store, she finds that food prices are up 9 per cent. General Foods will not bring down the price of groceries by next fall. Even though the government is trying to penalize farmers and fishermen by controlling their income, transportation costs and home heating costs are going up. They have been going up continuously. Energy costs will rise by 24 per cent as a result of deliberate government policy.
There is little money left in the family cheque for child care. Of course, working parents cannot deduct the cost of child care for income tax purposes. Obviously there is little money left for clothing. There is no money left for holidays for the woman worker struggling to raise her family. Bill C-124 will reduce wages by 6 per cent, bringing the wages of women even lower. They are already the lowest paid employees in the public service, and most will remain in those ghettos.
The next concern about this bill as it affects women workers in the public service-and this is an example of workers in all sectors of the economy-is the whole question of affirmative action rights, the right to equal job oportunities in the public service for men and women. Affirmative action will not be negotiated under Bill C-124. This is a very serious aspect of this bill. At first, people may not think so. However, I hope that members will think about it very seriously. It will restrict the chance for women to have equal jobs in the public service and equal rates of pay at the very time when an increasing number of women are being, or are about to be, laid off because of technological change.
Let us not kid ourselves: there are changes in every public department in practically every office which has anything to do with government services. In those offices, of course, are the women workers who will be laid off or through attrition are not being replaced. So it is most important that there be very firm affirmative action policies in place so that the jobs that are here are equally shared and together men and women can work for protection for workers in a positive way to counteract the negative effects of technological change.
In my question to the minister on July 6, I accused the President of the Treasury Board of denying women workers the right to bargain for affirmative action. I do not think he really heard or chose to hear the question; certainly he avoided answering it. Undoubtedly he is embarrassed by the very disgraceful record of this government on affirmative action.
It was the Treasury Board and, of course, the President of the Treasury Board who were supposed to be providing the leadership to establish a whole new progressive policy of affirmative action. You will recall that they started in three public departments, one of them being Treasury Board. They started a study and were going to implement changes that would be a model for all of Canada. Mr. Speaker, nothing whatsoever has happened. We have studies. We have had studies before. We know what few jobs in the higher paid category there are for women, but nothing is being done about it. Under Bill C-124 there will be no collective bargaining, so
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
workers and unions will have no chance. They will be prohibited from negotiating strongly for this very essential policy that we must have in the public service.
Let us look at all the facts concerning women in public service fields of employment. An excellent article appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on July 9. I recommend it to all hon. members. The article quoted the Public Service Commission Annual Report. It stated that only 4.3 per cent of public service executives, the top-ranking employees, are women. Only 4.3 per cent after all these years. Also, there are very few women in middle-management positions. Only 3.1 per cent of those earning over $50,000 are women. This represents an actual decrease over the past year, not an increase under affirmative action but a decrease. There has been almost no change in the position of women in the higher paid jobs in the public service from the 1970s, despite the many competent and experienced women who are in the public service and who should have opportunities for advancement.
According to Bonnie Carroll, who is from the Public Service Alliance, the equal opportunities program has not gone far enough. As a matter of fact, she says, it has not even gone anywhere. There is no teeth in it. There has been a rather polite program. She stated that in effect there has been no improvement in equal opportunities for women in the public service field.
This is really a very sad commentary, Mr. Speaker, on a government which has heard from so many women's groups, and from men as well, across the country who fought for equal rights in the Constitution. There were women who came back a second time to have Section 28 reinstated so that the provinces and the federal government could not override Section 15. It is a very sad commentary for ministers and leading departments who gave lip service to affirmative action and said that it must be compulsory.
Time and time again on this side of the House-at least, in this party, not in the party to our right-we have questioned those same ministers about affirmative action and asked what they were going to do to make it compulsory. The only way to ensure equal rights for women in the workplace is really to have mandatory affirmative action. At first there were three members who stood up, including the minister responsible for the status of women, and said: "We are all for mandatory affirmative action; we need it in the public service departments themselves and in government departments and we also need it in private sectors."
We pushed them on this and asked: "Every time you give out a government contract, why cannot you require affirmative action as part of the deal you have with the private sector, who are getting these jobs and getting paid by government?" However, how long did they stand up and really try to fight for mandatory affirmative action? No time at all. Very quickly after cabinet ministers had laid down the law-and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) undoubtedly-the minister responsible for the status of women was saying: "We really cannot do this right now; we cannot be too tough on the private

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
employees, we have to wait for this two or three-year study in the public departments, so we really cannot get on with affirmative action."
Therefore, it is not really surprising that this government, supported by the official opposition to my right, has brought in Bill C-124. It will protect the regressive status quo for women workers. It will prevent unions from bargaining aggressively for affirmative action to give women an equal place in the federal work force.
What about equal pay for work of equal value? I mentioned this in the House the other day, and the government side responded, obviously concerned about this, the day after. This is a major right which is threatened by Bill C-124. I have already documented the low wages which are paid to most women workers in the public service who work in job ghettos. However, not only do women not have an opportunity for advancement, but they are often paid lower wages than those of men working in similar types of jobs.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that last year a very significant battle was won when 3,000 general service workers, most of them female workers, won equal pay for work of equal value under the provisions of the Canada Human Rights Act. This was a very historic decision. The President of the Treasury Board, the instigator of this bill we are debating today, after first refusing to comply with the decision of the Human Rights Commission, was eventually forced to pay out $17 million in back pay to these service workers. Many of them were workers in cafeterias and in maintenance jobs. They had been paid some $2,000 to $3,000 less than male workers in similar categories. Female librarians also last year fought and won their case for pay equal to male librarians.
Right now, Mr. Speaker, there is a very important case before the Human Rights Commission, which we hope will rule in favour of hospital workers. Many hospital workers are female workers, of course, and are on very low rates of pay. There is very serious concern that under Bill C-124, Clause 8, this whole case before the Human Rights Commission, which is an equal pay for work of equal value case, will be endangered. Clauses 6 and 8 of this bill state that all other government acts can be overruled, so presumably Section 11(1) of the Canadian Human Rights Act itself will be overruled. The government may even override the Constitution, the Charter of Rights, which supposedly protects women against discrimination based on sex.
On July 7 the minister, attempting to clarify my question of the previous day, said that he would move on to enforce this section. Wookie-doo! In view of his past record of broken promises where women's rights are involved, we are very seriously concerned that his word is not good enough. I am sure the women of Canada are concerned, and the National Action Committee on the Status of Women I know are equally concerned.
The minister must withdraw the bill, since it is so harmful to public service workers in many respects. Legal advisers of NAC are also concerned that this bill contravenes the Human
Rights Act. Even if the minister amends the bill, the question of the rights of employees in Crown corporations still remains. Crown corporations might very well appeal this measure and have the Human Rights Act provision overruled.
If the minister is serious in his proclamations, he will not just amend this bill but withdraw it in favour of women workers and public service workers generally.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Women are becoming increasingly disenchanted with the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola), who happens also to have a secondary portfolio tacked on-her responsibility for the status of women. She is the minister of mines who undermines women. This minister is an all-talk-noaction minister. It is time she realized that charm and PR are simply not enough to advance women's rights in Canada.
I want to put on the record today at least five different incidents. This minister was appointed to work aggressively for the improvement of the status of women in Canada. She has made promises which she has either broken or on which she has refused to act in any meaningful way.
First, there was the whole Constitution debate. The minister reponsible for the status of women said to women who came to her that they should not worry. She did not say "dear," but it almost sounded like that. She told them the government would look after them and that Section 15 is all right. She told them she did not think they needed to worry that the provinces would override equal rights for women. Fortunately, the ad hoc women, who organized and were very expert on this question, realized the minister was wrong and they fought hard to get Section 28 in the Constitution.
Second is the question of pensions. This is the minister who took a very tough stand and promised action on women's pensions within one year. As we all know, this is a very urgently needed reform because pensioners are suffering. Women pensioners in particular are suffering, especially those living alone who in most cases are living below the poverty line. However, it is this particular minister who has supported this budget and this bill which would cut back cost of living indexing for pensioners. This, of course, will hit women pensioners the hardest because they are the poorest group.
Third, the minister promised to rescind Section 12(1 )(b) of the Indian Act, which discriminates against Indian women. Nothing has happened in that regard and, if the minister does not start soon, nothing ever will.
Fourth, the minister came out strongly in favour of mandatory affirmative action and then backed down and said: "We can't do it."
Finally, the minister has said she supports Bill C-124. In fact, in the past she has said that women in the public sector are "doing nicely" compared with women in the private sector. However, figures tell us that women in the public sector are doing exactly the same as, or perhaps even worse than, those in
