the private sector because they are still in occupationally segregated job ghettos. This is reflected in their pay scales, just as it is in the private sector. This minister has a lot of accounting to do to the women of Canada.
In the time I have left I want to refer to other changes in this bill which will be particularly hard on women workers. Many, many collective bargaining rights will be denied by Bill C-124. Women will be denied the right to negotiate health and safety matters and particularly the whole impact of VDTs and similar kinds of electronic equipment which pose very serious health risks, particularly for women workers. Women workers are faced with spending long hours working at this equipment and in environmental conditions which are quite dangerous and a risk to their health. It is essential, then, that unions on behalf of all workers, and particularly women workers, bargain collectively for safe and healthy working conditions and job security, which is threatened by technological change. This will not be allowed under Bill C-124.
Recently I attended a conference on technological change. The conference was about women and the impact of microtechnology. It was held here in Ottawa on June 25. Women came from all across Canada representing many organizations. At the end of the conference they endorsed a charter of rights to protect workers from the impacts of technological changes. I want to refer to the seven points they endorsed. I feel very strongly about them, and I know my party will feel they should be part of collective agreements with the federal government right now.
The first point is that all technological changes must be negotiated between unions and management. Bill C-124 will not allow that.
Second, employers are responsible to inform workers about all proposed technological changes. Workers and unions must have access to all information about types of change, types of equipment proposed and the likely health effects.
Third, there should be no reduction in the work force because of technological change, and the federal government has a responsibility to protect the jobs of women in particular.
Fourth, employers should be compelled to invest in retraining. The federal government must be planning and retraining workers who will be phased out of their present jobs for new skills and for non-traditional areas of work so that they will have jobs in the future.
Fifth, there must be limits on deskilling. Jobs must be broken down into smaller components.
Sixth, there must be strong health and safety protections.
Seventh-and this is very important for all federal departments-technological changes must be introduced step by step and phased in rather than being instituted all at once, allowing no chance for negotiations and planning on matters which involve workers and their unions.
I urge the federal government to adopt this charter. That is unlikely to happen because we do not believe the minister when he says his voluntary association for employees and

Another thing which will not be negotiable is parental leave. Over the past couple of years two public unions have won paid maternity leave for women workers after very tough fights. We know this would not have happened if these women had not had their unions and if they had not been militant about it. Under Bill C-124 parents who want and need time off for the birth of a child and for early parenting will have no union rights to negotiate for this. It is the dark ages again under Trudeau, MacEachen and Johnston. There will be loss of benefits in all areas and there will be no chance for workers to negotiate for these.

It is easy to adopt the Prime Minister's attitude. It is very easy to take advantage of the backlash against the public service of Canada because in some cases wage increases have been out of line. In many cases people in the public service are receiving salaries greater than they would in the private sector. But that is not to say that the public service is the author of the economic misfortune we have in Canada. We have to be very careful when we look at legislative measures such as Bill C-124 to try to remedy this situation. We want to be very careful that the prescription is directed at the right patient. We do not want simply to assume that the public service is contributing to inflation and by crushing down on the public service we are going to limit or in any way control inflation. I do not believe that, and I do not think too many members of this House really believe that if we do that, there will be any great changes taking place in Canada.
I can say without any fear of contradiction that what we really have to establish in Canada is a spirit of voluntary restraint. We have to convince Canadians that spending by government has gone too far and has to be limited or our inflation will continue.
However, Mr. Speaker, we do have to convince Canadians first of the correctness of a course of action. We have to ask Canadians to participate voluntarily in applying a remedy, which of course involves limited wage increases. But using legislation to ram it down the throats of Canadians has very small chance of working. In fact, it will work only if Canadians in the public service and the private sector willingly co-operate in what the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) described as a crusade. It is unfortunate that he used the terminology "a crusade". I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, from my reading of history, that no one was conscripted into a crusade. They were asked to volunteer because a crusade, by definition, appealed to those who believed in its purpose, that is what a crusade is, and I cannot point out the error of the government's ways any better than that. The government uses the word "crusade" to apply to a mandatory program of wage controls when the whole purpose of a crusade is to understand it, believe in it, endorse it, and participate voluntarily.
The government has sunk so low that it cannot make that kind of appeal any more. It cannot call in the leaders of the public service and say: "Will you co-operate with us in a crusade for the betterment of Canada and Canadians?" This government has sunk so low and the regard in which the government is held by the public service is at such a level that that kind of rapport cannot take place. That is a shame and that is the shame of this legislation, because Canadians, the Government of Canada and its employees cannot get together to resolve an evident problem. Instead, the problem has to be resolved by force of legislation.
I want to look very briefly at the background of the public service. I have said that there was an idea abroad in Canada that the public service, over a long period of time, has forced its salaries and benefits upward beyond those provided in the private sector. I do not know what the exact scientific comparisons are today, but I can tell you this, that the federal public service won the right to bargain collectively only in 1967. The process has been going on for only 15 years.
The Public Service Staff Relations Act was passed on February 14, 1967. The history of this process is quite recent. Not only that, the Liberal Government of Canada in 1977 through the medium of Bill C-28 and again in 1978 through the medium of Bill C-22 tried to break that collective bargaining process. In 1977 and 1978 we went through a process which was known among those concerned with the process as federal public service bashing.
The provisions of Bill C-28 in 1977 and Bill C-22 in 1978 were designed to provide another method of determining the salaries of federal public servants beyond the collective bargaining process. The device to be used was a pay research board which would determine each public servant's salary and what each class of public servant's salary ought to be. I well remember the outcry and uproar that came from the public servants and their representatives against these two bills. Many of us sat down and talked to them about these provisions and it transpired that there was a tremendous need for consultation in these areas, because the only way to resolve labour difficulties is through a consultative process.
I would have thought that the Liberal Government of Canada, through its experiences in 1977 and 1978 with its amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act, would have learned a lesson. I would have thought that the Liberal government would have learned that the way to get along with the Public Service of Canada is to consult with its representatives, not to present legislative measures and then try to ram them down their throats. That only invites confrontation and opposition. Apparently the Liberal government has not learned that lesson. Apparently the Liberal Government of Canada has not learned anything from its sad performance in past years and from its deteriorating relationships with the Public Service of Canada, because here we are faced with Bill C-124 at a time when all Canadians are agreeable to restraint measures.
Canadians have finally realized, and it took a $20 billion deficit to make them realize, that the federal government is spending too much money, and this is causing problems for all Canadians. It causes problems when Canadians go to the bank to borrow for a new car. It causes problems when home owners' mortgages expire and renewals must be negotiated. This situation is causing problems right across the economy for small-business men, farmers and fishermen. The Government of Canada is in the market borrowing too much money and this is driving interest rates upward. The provincial governments are right there beside the federal government at the same trough. In that situation, what chance has the consumer,
July 13, 1982

the home owner, the small-business man, the farmer or the fisherman to pay the kind of interest rates which this demand on the market creates?
As I indicated, Mr. Speaker, 1 think Canadians are beginning to get some grasp of these problems and are realizing that there is a solution to them. It may well be that, properly approached, not only public servants but all those in the private sector could be convinced that the way out and the solution is certainly, in part, restraint on wage increases.
I have no difficulty explaining to Canadians to whom I speak that it is much better to receive a 6 per cent increase and have an inflation rate of 6 per cent than to receive a 10 per cent increase with an inflation rate of 11 per cent. I do not think you have to take too much time to explain that because with the experience Canadians have had over the last decade, the deteriorating value of the dollar, the dramatic increases in food and services, the dramatic increases in the cost of housing and other essential things, they now realize a dollar is no longer worth a dollar. It is not even worth 40 cents any more.
I think the time has now come in Canada when you can reach out and tell Canadians what is happening and deal with them in a realistic way. The real point is, do you do that by beating their heads with a hammer, or by convincing them that the right course of action is to exercise constraint on a volunteer basis? But that kind of opportunity unfortunately was thrown away by the introduction of budgetary measures of the Minister of Finance on June 28 and by the legislation that he will introduce to implement them. Bill C-124 is only the first step.
I have to remind my colleagues to the left in the New Democratic Party that they did the Public Service of Canada and all organized labour in Canada a disservice when they objected to the inclusion in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms of a provision that would guarantee property and related rights to all Canadians. Because if the Public Service Alliance and other public service unions had a guarantee of property rights and related rights through a constitutional provision, the Government of Canada would not now be able to reverse those contracts as it intends to do.

Let me go on record as saying that I am in favour of legislation which is generally beneficial although it may have some flaws. I work to improve legislation like the freedom of information legislation and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I want them to be enacted, I want Canadians to have the benefit of those provisions which are beneficial. I am not like the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) who held up, in the House of Commons and in the committee of the House of Commons, the freedom of information legislation to the point where it was not going to be passed. Canadians have suffered for the last year and a half because the hon. member for Burnaby, a member of the New Democratic Party, stood in committee and refused to allow passage of that bill which would have given all kinds of

Canadians access to all kinds of information. This is what we call cutting off your nose to spite your face: to refuse to deal with a minor provision of a large piece of legislation. I want to make it very clear to members of the New Democratic Party that I do not believe in that approach. I believe that if it is basically good I am prepared to support it.
As the late Right Hon. John Diefenbaker said, "You don't follow rabbit tracks when you are after big game", so I will get back to Bill C-124 and deal with each provision which may be found to be onerous by a great many public servants. This bill not only affects 500,000 public servants, including those in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Canadian Armed Forces and others employed by Crown corporations and agencies, but it affects public servants in provincial spheres and eventually it will affect public servants in municipal spheres. I believe that it will have an effect upon all institutional employees across Canada, whose institutions are supported by government funds. That includes hospitals, universities and a wide variety of similar institutions. When we talk about the Canadians affected by this bill, we are not talking about the 500,000 federal public servants, including members of the RCMP and the Canadian Armed Forces, we are talking about another
500,000	Canadians, 300,000 of whom are in provincial public services and 200,000 of whom are in municipal services. In addition, we are talking about probably another 500,000 persons who are employed in institutions like hospitals and post-secondary educational institutions as well as public schools.
There is a broad interest and concern with this bill. It is for that reason that it demands serious consideration by all members of the House. Also it demands us to inquire whether the provisions of the bill are fair and proper in the circumstances. This is the question which I now want to address-is this bill and its provisions fair and proper in the circumstances?
Of course, and unfortunately for the Government of Canada, for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and for the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) who flies back and forth wasting money all the time, the bill is not fair. It is patently unfair because it takes a 6 per cent criterion and applies it to a deputy minister receiving $100,000 per year. It takes the same 6 per cent criterion and applies it to a clerk making $13,000, $14,000 or $15,000 per year, if there are any of those people in the Public Service of Canada any more. How can we support a provision which says that the government will limit Michael Pitfield to a $6,000 increase and at the same time limits a $15,000 per year clerk to the same 6 per cent increase? It is patently unfair.
I do not think anyone on the government side of the House would dare stand up and say that that kind of legislative provision is fair. How could they possibly say that it is fair? They know that lower level employees, those receiving less funds from the federal public service, the Canadian Armed Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and all federal corporations, are battling against an inflation rate which is over 12 per cent. They are battling in some places to renew their mortgages at 19 per cent, 20 per cent and 21 per cent.
They are battling with increases in true prices. They are battling to pay increased transportation costs, increased costs of transportation fuels. They know the problem exists, so how can they go to these people and say that they will be giving them the same wage increase limit as they are giving Mr. Michael Pitfield who was already paid $110,000 when he left his job, whom they already sent all over the world and flew down to Boston to visit his family, and who was given all those benefits, which he has probably blown away, amounting to $100,000 or $200,000? How can they apply the same rule to these two persons?
When the Government of Canada tries to do something like that, no wonder public service unions and labour representatives of the public service rise up and complain. No wonder they send around material to Members of Parliament and form an Inter-Union Committee Against Wage Controls. No wonder they complain that Bill C-124 violates International Labour Organization conventions. No wonder they are upset. No wonder they are contemplating actions which would probably be detrimental not only to the public service itself but to all Canadians. They recognize that that kind of unfairness is patent and cannot be tolerated. If they take that kind of action and do not react to it, they know that they will be emasculating their organizations for all times.
What about the other side of the coin? Are public servants to rise up and revolt through their union representatives? Are they to join with the Canadian Labour Congress and Mr. Dennis McDermott and knock down the walls of Parliament in order to get the government to change its view? We certainly do not want that, and we certainly do not encourage any such confrontations. But they should not back someone into the corner. They should allow them some room within which to manoeuvre. That room could have been given to the public service in the form of allowing for some kind of graduated scale of increases which would take into account the large amounts received by those at the top. Also it could have taken into account the small amounts received by those at the bottom. But to force upon the public service an across-the-board 6 per cent limit is to challenge them and to say, "We will make you the scapegoats of our restraint program; we will organize public opinion against you, the public servant." It will not help them, it will not help Canadians. It will not help the private sector or even those executive officers of private corporations who think that there may be some benefit to setting an example and that they will be able to use the same guidelines. It will not work that way because, if we do not know anything else about constitutional law, we know that you can lead a horse to water but you cannot make him drink.
That is what will happen in the public service if these restrictions and restraints are forced upon its employees. They will simply cut back and will not produce. They will find methods not to comply with the commands of their superiors and at the same time to avoid loss of employment. It will set a pattern in the public service which will bring the country, if not to a standstill then something very close to it.
The government has taken a very dangerous course of action. Given the course of action which the government has
July 13, 1982

taken, one which is obviously wrong in the sense that it wipes away 15 years of effective collective bargaining and wipes away any sense of comparability or fairness in wage packages,
I say to members of the public service inside or outside the House that they must realize the level to which the Government of Canada has sunk. I say to them, "Do not blame Parliament or Canadians for what is happening to the Public Service of Canada. It is the fault of the Government of Canada." As I said, it simply indicates the level to which the government, that group of persons, has sunk that it would try this kind of action.
What is the hope for the future? The hope for the future is that in two years' time-and hopefully earlier-there will be a general election and the people of Canada will no longer have to put up with the government and its errant ways. Then the public service will be able to look forward to a situation in the future in which it will be treated in a decent and fair manner by the government of the day, which will not be the Liberal government. Also I suggest to the public service and its leaders that they should not react violently without regard for the welfare of other Canadians faced with the piece of legislation contained in Bill C-124. But consider beyond the narrow and short-term future to a future in which they will perhaps see a different kind of government, a different kind of attitude on the part of government, a different respect for employees of the Government of Canada, a government that will recognize the value of consultation and recognize that the way for an employer to deal with an employee is to sit down and work out the problems which may exist between them for the benefit of all Canadians, not only for that of the employer and employee.
I would like to close with just one example of a relationship between an employer and his employees that came to the point of total collapse. It concerned the Canadian postal service. What did this Parliament do? We terminated the Canadian postal service and created a new corporation called Canada Post. I want to look around this House and the nation and ask everyone whether they can see any difference in the service provided by Canada Post since its creation. I see no difference in the service, and I do not mean to criticize its management, nor do I want to criticize my postman, your postman and the postal employees upon whom I must depend a great deal of the time. The fact is, there is no difference in the service.
The point I want to make is that these kinds of changes are superficial and meaningless. When one is dealing with people, it must be on a proper basis. One must respect the people with whom one is dealing. One must listen to their opinions and respect their judgments. One must deal with them on a humane basis. One cannot merely bring into the House of Commons a piece of paper saying that one will do this and that, because people will not pay any attention to pieces of paper. What people pay attention to are sensible rules and regulations. What employees pay attention to is an employer who provides sensible rules and regulations governing the
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
terms and conditions of their employment and their remuneration. Unless the Government of Canada learns that lesson, unless it sits down with the public service and enacts sensible rules and regulations governing their employment and remuneration, there will be no peace in the Public Service of Canada. The message I want to bring to Members of Parliament is that the way to a solution is through consultation, not through arbitrary, statutory action.

It is clear 1 am rising to speak against Bill C-124. I do not hide in a lot of rhetoric how I plan to vote on this piece of legislation. I make it clear from the very start because it seems to be a weapon for use against inflation, but it is certainly far from that. It is certainly no more than a vicious attack on the clerical staff, teachers, policemen, military personnel and others who provide much needed public services across Canada. They as a group are already paid below what their contemporaries receive in the private sector. There is no doubt that wage demands are a factor in the process of inflation. However, the 11 per cent inflation we find today is, at root, a social phenomenon. It results from a wide array of social problems in our economy and in society generally. It is a reflection of the competition and the process of distribution of the total goods and services produced in Canada.
Any effective solution for dealing with inflation must attack the problem at its roots in the underlying structure of our economy. The open adoption of the monetarist and neoKeynesian solution by the Liberals and Conservatives at this time clearly defines for Canadians the fundamental difference in approach taken by the NDP on economic matters. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) says, "Successive reductions in money income demands will be required year by year if declining inflation is to be achieved", many Canadians are right in rejecting such rubbish. It is clear beyond any doubt that the road to economic security is predicated upon a much greater degree of democratic control over basic investment decisions which determine the timing and direction of our economic growth.
I am pleased to have an opportunity to place on the record some facts about Bill C-124, contrary to what hon. members involved in the Liberal-Tory coalition have been doing here today. It has been clear from the very start in the comments of the leaders of the Liberal and Tory parties that those parties support the smashing of collective rights. Joe says that it is a step in the right direction and Pierre says that it is necessary to show that he is serious. Well, if isolating less than 5 per cent of the work force for economic punishment is fairness and leadership, then those two parties have more serious problems of political dishonesty and senility than most Canadians have suspected to date. Why not isolate men between the ages of 40 and 45, 5'10" tall, weighing 165 pounds, with brown hair and blue eyes, to be the victims? It is in that very metaphor that the truth lies. It is in polls, used extensively by the right wing parties in this country, to support their ill-founded theories. Many Canadians believe that public servants are lazy, stupid, overpaid, overpensioned, in positions where they cannot be fired, with unlimited job security.

My friend, the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), says that it is Tory policy. That is very interesting. But today I have had an opportunity to meet with the representatives of the trade unions of CN, and I found that the problem which has been created by Bill C-124 in relation to the collective agreement jointly shared with CP will create an
incredible amount of chaos on the railroads and in the transportation sector of this country. It will do untold harm, not only to grain shipments out of Canada but also to interpersonal relationships between railroaders. It has long been held that they all bargain in terms of a private sector agreement, and some very unfortunate incidents will occur in relation to railroads as a result of Bill C-124.
Before I was interrupted by the hon. member, I was pointing out that many Canadians believe that public servants do not do a great deal of work, that they cannot be fired and have unlimited job security. Many of these same Canadians who believe that sleep a little better if they know the public servants are having to accept lower pay and suffer, even if unfairly, at the hands of government. However, let us look behind the myths. I noticed here today quite a few smirking faces among the Liberals and the Conservatives. They know how right I am that the honesty of Bill C-124 is not the issue. The politics of supporting it and collecting the public credit is all that the Liberal-Tory coalition is about.
Let us look for a moment at a public servant earning $12,000 a year. That is not at all uncommon either here in Ottawa or across the country. Next year, rather than getting an increase tied to inflation, he or she will get 6 per cent. If that person has a loan on a car at 20 per cent or 21 per cent, it will still be at 20 per cent or 21 per cent next year. A mortgage will likely run in the low 20 per cent range. Inflation has been introduced structurally into the Canadian economy, and that fact was accepted in all the figures put before this house by the Minister of Finance. It is for that reason we have to look very carefully at Bill C-124 and the philosophy that is behind it.
Forcing that individual to take a real loss in income for a sixth and seventh year in a row is both savage and unnecessary. The business community has somewhat reluctantly come forward again to praise Bill C-124 as a good start, much as the Conservatives have. Sure profits are generally down, and when they are down, business is very co-operative with government, looking for any handouts, loans, legislation or whatever they can get their hands on. It is a different story when the economy is flush. Business is quick to move capital out of the reach of workers and government alike.
The public and workers must help bail out Massey-Fergu-son, Dome, Imperial, Consolidated Computer-a loss which alone would be able to provide the financial and wage requirements for the existing public service contracts. The list is endless. When has a corporation in this country ever given the public purse a comparable return to what they take when times are hard? It is not likely and it is not ever likely as long as the Liberal-Tory coalition is in power in this country.
How long will it be before Joe and Pierre come out of the closet, or should I say Allan and John, the friendly financiers? How long before we see the coalition of various and sundry right-wingers as we have in British Columbia? After all,
July 13, 1982

Socreds are nothing more than an unhealthy alliance of Liberals and Conservatives.
How many of those same Canadians who dislike public servants are aware of the fact that in this session alone the Tories have voted 33 times to keep the Liberals in power? The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) 1 am sure feels very guilty, being the only Tory here to carry the blame for his party for having continually supported the government, keeping it in power day after day after day. I wonder if your constituents know, Frank, how dearly you love to keep Pierre Trudeau in office.

The Liberals are so deep in the swamp of intellectual and political dishonesty that to describe their integrity as a roorback is a compliment.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
Let us look for a moment at the bill and see what is in it. In the application section we see under subclause (1) that it is going to apply to employees in all departments or ministries of state of the Government of Canada, boards, commissions or corporations, the Canadian Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Senate and the House of Commons. Subclause 2 applies to staffs of ministers of the Crown and of members of the House of Commons and the Senate. The third subclause applies to persons appointed by the governor in council. Clause 4, the extension section, reads:
Every compensation plan that is in effect on June 28, 1982 for employees to whom this part applies, including every compensation plan extended under Section 5, shall be extended for the period of twenty-four months.
Then we get to a couple of interesting sections. Clause 6(2) is called an exception. It reads:
The Treasury Board may, where it deems it appropriate, authorize any change to any terms and conditions, other than wage rates, of a compensation plan that would, but for Section 5, have expired before June 28, 1982.
Perhaps, for the learning experience of the Liberals and Tories still in the chamber, they should read that clause and get some understanding of it. It means that Treasury Board can change the actual working components of a collective agreement, not just wages alone. It is called contract busting.
Then there is Clause 13 which is when, as a result of the six and five policies, in some areas of the public service sector, we get to the point where there is no one left in some areas of the departments, special powers are given to Treasury Board. It states as follows:
The governor in council may, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, by order,
(a) substitute, in respect of a compensation plan or a class of compensation
plans, a percentage different from that set out in paragraph 9(1 )(b), where he
considers it in the public interest to do so on grounds of labour shortages;
Employees can be hired above the six and five, but only after those departments have been completely bilked by a rate of attrition. It is interesting, in looking back on the public record, as I have been doing in the last few days, to see what was said by all parties in this House about collective bargaining and the right to strike during the rise in popularity of Solidarity in Poland. The Liberals and Conservatives all touted themselves as the true supporters of trade unions, touted their policy that trade unions were the fundamental basis or cornerstone of freedom, particularly in the Eastern Bloc.
They have now received word that the Gallup poll reveals otherwise in Canada, and there goes their support. Their bottom line is that collective bargaining and the right to strike is good for the Soviet Union but not so good for Canada. When Commie-bashing is in, the Tories are all up on their feet and so are the Liberals. At that point human rights and collective rights are the order of the day. When profits are down and the Gallup shifts in Canada, so too goes the rightwing Liberal-Tory coalition.
Opinion polls do in fact show that two out of three Canadians believe that unions are too powerful, this opinion being a result of continued misinformation provided to the public by the media, the government and big business. When was the

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
last time a group of loggers, or fishermen owned The Globe and Mail? Liberal and Tory governments particularly like to bargain in bad faith and to introduce bills such as Bill C-124. They love to dare public service unions to strike or fight back. They know that only the public will be hurt, and the public has historically always blamed the unions, not the government. That seems to be a quick way of trying to get back into office.
Thus we start to see the reason behind Bill C-124. It is not to try to bring down inflation, not to bring down interest rates, not to show the way for the settlement of private contracts for the next two years. The reasoning is tragically dishonest. Union-busting is popular with the public, and the Liberals are clutching at anything because they have allowed our national economy to reach the stage where in fact for many it has already collapsed. subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to continue speaking against Bill C-124, and I hope that in the days and weeks coming we will have an opportunity to hear from the Liberals and the Conservatives as to why they support this legislation. With 1.3 million unemployed officially and perhaps another 1 million out of work, there are four or five times the number out of work as there are affected by Bill C-124. Rather than argue the merits of a major plan for job creation or economic stimulation, we are here in this House debating the values of punishing public servants for the mistakes of an incompetent government.
What kind of politicians, Mr. Speaker, single out the victims to blame? This kind of action, taking purchasing power away from workers and consumers, is not even a stopgap measure. It is precisely the same kind of chiselling as in the budget, taking $1.3 billion away from low and middle-income earners by hiking the income tax. Bill C-124 is, in my view, a floater, to assess public reaction to full-blown wage controls. This is a plan that no doubt the Liberals are hurriedly preparing for the October Speech from the Throne.
The slide and the depression over the summer will simply add fuel to the false premises of the Liberals and Conservatives that the root of the problem we have in Canada is wages. It is clear beyond any doubt that the high interest rates and the fundamental structure of Canada's externally manipulated economy are the cause of our problems. Cynically to manipulate public opinion into believing that wage controls will refloat Canada's economy is reprehensible.
The Department of Finance has been actively preparing the ground to save the face of the Minister of Finance from further sand and gravel burns with such documents as "Setting the Climate for Wage Controls". That document said, in part: "A strategy of controls could only be contemplated if the country was widely recognized as facing a major emergency."
Let us head on into the seedier side of this issue. Who stands to profit from continued high interest rates, the demolition of the Foreign Investment Review Agency, and wage controls? First, let us look at who encourages support for the high interest rates. It is none other than the Minister of Finance, with his 19.5 per cent Canada Savings Bonds. What better way for a street dealer in economic misery to find the equivalent of a downtown Vancouver junkie? It is a quick "fix" for a collapsing government and a psychological introduction of acceptance and desire for higher rates to tens of thousands of Canadians. Who really benefits from the higher rate? Only about 5 per cent of Canadians who have surplus thousands or millions of dollars to put in the bank. Who pays so that they can profit? The public servants, the workers, small business, the home owners, all pay roughly 20 per cent on borrowed money. This trend, Mr. Speaker, leads to a major realignment in the economy, with a small group gaining enormous economic advantage during times of inflation, high unemployment and general recession.
Wage controls simply shift part of the burden of a floundering, poorly-planned economy onto the backs of working and unemployed Canadians. It is high time that those corporations that have been shovelling billions of dollars in profits and dividends out of Canada, brought some back and helped to revitalize the economy that they have played a major role in upsetting. In one recent five-year period, Mr. Speaker, some of the large corporations took $32 billion worth of capital gain in Canada out of the country. Surely no thinking Canadian blames the problems of Massey-Ferguson on the meagre pay packet of the worker who instals tractor engines or sets the hydraulics on farm machinery? Surely it is time management took their share of the rap, and sat down with labour leaders, workers and small business and mapped out a means of bringing this economy into the twentieth century.
Why are interest rates three times those of Japan and West Germany? They are three times the interest rates and now almost three times the percentage of unemployed. Why is nothing done when the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs finds that the oil companies have ripped us off for $12 billion at the gas pump in recent years? Therein lies the answer, or at least part of it.
Let us look for a moment at restraint measures in the boardroom. I am sure many members to my right and across the floor have had a look at these, but I think it is worth putting them on the record, Mr. Speaker. For example, the President of Alcan, David Culver, received $392,000 in 1980, and his vision of restraint took him to $532,000 in wages last year, a jump of $ 140,000 in one year.
July 13, 1982

Bell Canada, who want a 25 per cent increase, certainly found that in the boardroom. Mr. Grandpre went from $514,000 to $626,00 in one year. Canadian Pacific, Mr. Burbidge, went from $318,000 to $457,000 in the last two years. Falconbridge Nickel, Mr. Cooper, did not get quite as much, but he went from $132,000 to $252,000 in one year, a jump of almost 100 per cent in pay. Husky Oil, Mr. L. M. Rasmussen, went from $296,000 to $378,000. There is a real kind of restraint. Ranger Oil, Mr. Pierce, went from $233,000 to $398,000. Westcoast Transmission, a good British Columbia company, Mr. E. Phillips, went from $257,000 to $444,000.
If that is restraint in the boardroom I would like to meet with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and say: "Wage controls on those Canadians earning $12,000 or less is really the way to go, to get in there and take that out of the hides of the poorly paid clerks and public service staff."
Economists have noted that, "This recession has been unique in serveral respects. An examination of the cause of the downturn rather than its effect show it to be a recession deliberately brought about and fostered by government to a degree that has not occurred before." That is a quotation from Peter Cook of The Globe and Mail of April 17, 1982.
The Liberals and the Conservatives both operate now, Mr. Speaker, on opinion polls-no matter if the polls reflect the basic misunderstanding of facts. The 1982 Goldfarb report said the following, and I am sure that this is the foundation stone of Bill C-124: "There is a desire to see some measure of punishment of the civil service ... a feeling that it is some sort of elite group . . . that has insulated itself from the hard economic realities of the day."
Some examples are deserving of scrutiny so that all members of this House, when they vote for or against this bill, will know why. Here are some examples from salaries in 1981: typists in the public sector, $11,658, and in the private sector on average, $12,226; labourers in the public sector, $15,611, and in the private sector, $17,197; financial administrators, public sector, $40,458, and in the private sector, $52,002. Pay scales, Mr. Speaker, in the public sector are consistently lower than in the private sector.
The Prime Minister demonstrated his government's total insincerity in Banff on June 20 of this year by saying that he would "scare the hell out of people by creating more unemployment," if they failed to respond to his dictates. In the past week the Prime Minister has threatened mandatory controls, denied the threat, apologized for the threat, and then restated the threat. We are dealing with the same Liberal-Conservative strategy as in 1974-75, a campaign promise not to bring in controls and then swiftly bring in wage controls.
This government, hand in hand with the Tories in this House and with all the provinces except Manitoba, is deliberately bringing in policies which put people out of work. We have a staggering 1.3 million out of work officially and another
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
1 million unofficially out of work because they are no longer collecting unemployment insurance or are on the "active list".
Bill C-124 breaks existing contracts; let us not forget that, especially when the impact will be to push some federal employees, such as clerks, below the poverty line. I am sure hon. members of this House have seen recent articles respecting members of the public service who have gone to welfare offices across the country and, in fact, get more take-home pay by being on welfare than working for the public service. This happens in the military as well.
By contrast, let any Liberal or Tory rise and inform this House of a 6 per cent or 5 per cent rollback of loans, mortgages, oil prices, electricity, water, rent or anything else. And let us not forget that there are eight Tory premiers who support this kind of thinking wholeheartedly. There is silence, and perhaps for good reason. There are some interesting parallels between the Liberals and the Conservatives on economic direction and high interest rates. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the previous minister of finance in the Tory government, said the following in a CTV interview on June 7, 1981:
Yes I would continue to back Mr. Bouey. I agree that our interest rates have to track those in the United States.
The previous prime minister, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), was reported by The Toronto Star on May 5 of this year as saying:
We have looked for a solution other than the government's, but we couldn't come up with an alternative ... At this moment I don't have a better solution.
No doubt the Leader of the Opposition is having trouble with his leadership.
On honesty in federal politics, on "The Watson Report" on February 4, 1979, the hon. member for St. John's West said:
-our leaders have got to be a little less honest ... we're not being devious and tricky enough ... I am criticizing us for that.
What kind of political animal would say those things? The same previous minister of finance said, as recorded in Macleans magazine of July 12, 1982, that the government:
-is adrift; it has no answers. If I told you what I would do, we'd never get elected.
That is good Tory policy for you.
On controls on wages, the previous prime minister said the following on July 5 of this year:
What is in the budget? There is one important initiative-the introduction of restraint on public sector salaries.
Day after day we have seen Tories trying to dance around the issue. They have tried to speak in their ridings on behalf of the public service, yet knowing full well that the whips will be on and they will all have to vote for this Neanderthal legislation.
The Leader of the Opposition went on to say:
That is a field in which the government has lagged behind several Canadian provinces. We are relieved that it is beginning to accept that government spending is a major cause of current economic problems ... it is a step in the right direction.

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
That is Tory policy on Bill C-124. The Tories cannot dance around that any longer.
This kind of one-sided back-alley bludgeoning of collective agreements will, in my view, introduce a new and potentially explosive ingredient in employee-employer relations in this land. In my previous employment in the courts of B.C. and as a shop steward with a public service union I came to understand and appreciate the logo I think many of us know that justice must be done and be seen to be done. Bill C-124 is a completely unfounded Neanderthal approach to economics. Slamming the hands of the public service in the doorjamb may bring cries of support from some sectors of Canadian society; however, being seen to be just is a far cry from being just.
A 6 per cent rollback of the salary of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), whom I am glad to see here tonight, is more money than many Canadians make in a year. Let me give an example of the impact of the June 28 budget and Bill C-124 on a relatively well-paid federal employee. A clerk with two dependants earning $20,000 by 1984 will see the controls of 6 per cent and 5 per cent cost her $2,204 in salary. A 52 per cent increase in UIC premiums will cost another $300. Loss of full indexing of family allowance will cost another $104. Increasing taxes as a result of partial deindexing will cost another $450. A slight gain is the $100 child tax credit increase. All of this means a total cut over the next two years of $2,958, or 15 per cent of the original $20,000 salary. I just wonder how many Liberals and Tories will go back to their constituencies and say that is not a scandalous chopping of the public service they say they support.
The shoe, however, is on the other foot when it comes to higher income earners. The Liberal proposal is to offer investors taxation only on that return on investment which exceeds inflation. Thus, an investment of $20,000 at 12.2 per cent when inflation is running at 11 per cent would mean $2,200 of investment income would be protected from tax. At a marginal tax rate of 50 per cent this would mean a reduction in taxes of about $1,100.
It is clear that the advice given to the Liberals and accepted by them and the Tories is to control wages in the public sector first and then across the board this fall, thus increasing available capital to government and big business. Small business, workers, the elderly and the unemployed are expected to live on what they can find. High interest rates and low levels of taxation will allow an accelerated accumulation of capital, real estate and whatever by a small economic elite. It is no small coincidence that this group is similar to the list of campaign contributors to the Liberals and Conservatives.
In conclusion, let me touch on the highlights of the Reagan-Thatcher-Trudeau-Clark proposals.
Fact: Over 11 per cent of the work force is unemployed and, despite the expenditure of more federal funds in my riding, for example, in the past year and in the coming year than in any other federal riding in Canada, we now have 25 per cent unemployment due to accompanying federal policies. Nationally, industrial production is down 10 per cent. Real income is
down 10 per cent since 1976 and plant utilization is down 30 per cent, in some regions 50 per cent and in some industries, such as mining and forestry now, down 100 per cent.
The intent of the budget and Bill C-124 is to cause this income decline to accelerate, and that is based on quotes I have taken directly from the Minister of Finance.
The source of the current recession is an economic philosophy and practice, not Washington alone and not the cracked crystal ball of the Minister of Finance alone. When Canadians come to realize-and I truly hope it will not be from a dusty history book ten years from now-that this phony legislation of the Liberal-Tory coalition is designed to protect the wealthy few and some chosen business sectors, then the will and the sentiment of the country to be sovereign, secure and peaceful and to have a cornerstone of free collective bargaining will be unleashed, and most members of the Liberal-Tory coalition here today will be voted out of office.
Bill C-124 is a slice out of federal workers. Big business will demand extension of it by the Liberal-Tory coalition to all workers so that they can finance their corporate debt and liquidity problems. The question is whether workers, small business, the unemployed and the elderly will stand idly by while they lose their homes, their jobs and their dreams.
Also within Bill C-124 is the disposal of the right to strike. I think what the impact of removing this right from the public service means is important and worthy of very serious consideration. There is no doubt that the strike is the most misunderstood of social activities in Canada. Surveys historically have consistently concluded that Canadians view strikes as an abuse of union power and a restriction on their access to goods and services. There is however, no ready replacement for this tool. There is no less combative way of settling labour-management disputes. Many Canadians support removal of the right to strike from public service unions. In fact, some Canadians- as a matter of fact, some members to my right-support legislating unions out of existence completely.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Make a distinction.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
The far right, the Tories.
The myths which have allowed such opinions to develop require close scrutiny. It is a fact of history that unions have reduced the numbers of strikes globally. Deprived of unions, what useful vehicle would there be for the peaceful settlement of disputes over health and safety, technological change or many of the issues affecting workers every day when they are at work? Strikes would proliferate at a rate previously unknown in this country. Production and co-operation in the public sector may be lost already to absenteeism, staff turnover, slow-downs, shoddy work and so forth. If we take an hour's pay away from a worker without making consistent changes to the cost of living, we must expect-in fact we are encouraging-chaos. Something Liberal members should take into consideration when blindly supporting this legislation is that it will cause a chaos we probably have not seen in the public sector in the history of this country.
July 13, 1982

Strikes have been going on on this planet for the past 8,000 years, ever since the workers constructing the pyramids in Egypt walked off the job. Those countries governed by dictatorships which tightly control unions suffer from serious production losses due to unresolved employer-employee conflicts. Removal of the right to strike from public service unions is totally unacceptable. It is an invitation to civil disobedience.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I think members of the House might be interested in a couple of quotations that I should like to put on the record. The first is the words of Pope John Paul II who said:
The justice of any socioeconomic system deserves in the final analysis to be evaluated by the way in which work is properly compensated ... The organization of workers into unions is necessary to protect the rights of workers, especially the right to a just wage ... In this connection, workers should be assured the right to strike, without being subjected to personal penal sanctions for taking part in a strike.
Another interesting quotation comes from a well known labour mediator, Dr. Noel Hall, who said:
There's no sense in talking about banning strikes in the public sector. That will not make labour unrest disappear. All we would be doing is passing a law that otherwise good, law-abiding citizens would ignore . . . Nor is the answer to impose compulsory arbitration. The real problem with both methods is that they come dangerously close to a system of compulsory employment. We would be telling people: "You must set your alarm clock. You must get up. And you must go to work." Are we really willing to issue this kind of order?
When the Liberal and Conservative members rise to vote for this legislation, as they seem intent on doing, I hope that they will keep in mind that they are encouraging many of the
500,000	people in the public service unions of this country to become involved in civil disobedience. These people are normally law-abiding Canadians. It is a shameful thing to force any Canadian into that kind of trap.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have mixed feelings about speaking in this debate on second reading of Bill C-124, an act respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada. Before we can go into a study of this bill in depth we should look at some of the background to it.
I should like to address a few comments to the budget presented in this House by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on June 28. It was apparent from the minister's speech that evening that the budget had two objectives. The first was to bring down inflation and the second was to shore up investment and confidence in the economy.
With regard to the first objective, the government told us that it is going to point the way to recovery but that it cannot get going on its own. It told us that we must tackle this task together. I find it strange that members of the government would say that we have to work together to "beat inflation to the ground", at the same time that they are asking everyone else in the country to accept a 6 per cent wage increase in the 1982-83 fiscal year and a 5 per cent increase in the 1983-84 fiscal year. In that same period the government will increase its budget by 20 per cent. It seems to me that it is only paying
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
lip service to these objectives in order to try to impress upon the people the dire economic crisis that the country faces. It is true that the country faces a dire economic crisis but the government only pays lip service to it. If it were serioius it would not ask the Canadian people to accept a 6 per cent increase while it increases its own budget by 20 per cent.
We also have a serious problem when the government says that we must beat inflation to the ground at the same time as it introduces a budget with a deficit for this year of $19.6 billion. That in itself is not nearly as great a problem as the deficit accumulated in the years this government has been in power, which to date is estimated at $135 billion. We cannot tell how accurate that figure is because there is no place in government where it can be checked.
If the government is serious about beating inflation to the ground why, then, do we have an accumulated deficit of $135 billion? When it was in the area of $80 billion it took $1 in every $5 of government revenue to service the interest; now, with the amount at $135 billion it takes close to $2 in every $5 that the government raises to service the debt. Exactly. Some are in more than others. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) has said it and I fully agree with him. However, if a member of the House says there is no hope and predicts even greater failure, what hope do we have? What hope is there if members of Parliament cannot rally to the cause of inflation and the economic ills of the day? That is what we can expect from members of the NDP. Talk about promoting disunity.
As we know, the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) two weeks ago had as its main theme the fight against inflation-to bring inflation down to 6 per cent. This is the target for which we must strive. Federal public servants, Crown corporations, regulatory agencies as well as members of Parliament and senators are being asked to participate in this program. It is hoped that with this approach, the provinces, municipalities and the private sector as a whole will follow suit and join in this concerted effort to wrestle down inflation.
The intent of this bill, as we all know, is to limit wage increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent. It means that some
500,000	people in government and in Crown corporations will get no more than 6 per cent.
A very significant point, something we have to underline, is that this will free some $250 million this year and $550 million next year. That money can be spent on programs to stimulate the economy and create much needed jobs.
Members of the opposition, especially the NDP, fail to bring out the point that because of this particular program, nearly $800 million will be directed into much needed job-creation programs. This is without further adding to the current deficit which is of concern to all of us. There is no doubt about it, we have to wrestle down the deficit. However, we cannot get the deficit down until we get inflation and interest rates down. Therefore, we must all work together.
Let us hope that provincial and municipal governments look hard and long at the decision of the federal government in this matter. Let us hope that the big corporations, the utilities and the labour movement will consider this idea very carefully. If all sectors of society could agree voluntarily to the 6 per cent limit, we would bring inflation down and provide far more jobs that will be needed in the future.
Would it not be an outstanding achievement if, as Richard Gwyn said in his column today, we could see the emergence of a national will to defeat inflation? That is the intent of this government, to create the atmosphere for that national will to
July 13, 1982

take place so that we can defeat inflation, getting it down to a more reasonable rate of 6 per cent and, hopefully, then to 5 per cent.
The rate of recovery must begin with a realistic assessment of what this country is all about, what this country can control and what we cannot control. Our country cannot deal with its economic problems in isolation. We can ease if not eliminate the impact of some problems, but the solutions to other difficulties depend on events beyond our borders.
We must know what we can realistically change and what is beyond our power to change by ourselves. While recognizing the force of world conditions, we must acknowledge that many of our problems originate here at home. No doubt about it, we are responsible for many of the economic problems we face today. We cannot put all the blame on outside forces or world powers. An inflation rate of 11.8 per cent is far too high. Our cost structure is becoming prohibitive. To be honest, we are pricing ourselves out of world markets. We are losing our competitive edge. All this we have done to ourselves.
Rather than accept what the previous speaker said, voicing doom and gloom, I have confidence in the Canadian people. I have confidence that what we have done we can also turn around. We can reverse this trend. If we all work together, we can bring inflation down. The government is taking the lead by asking all those associated with the federal service to join in this battle against inflation and to take the lead themselves by limiting their wage expectations.
In many ways, expectations are at the heart of our inflation problems. In recent years it seemed natural for all of us to believe that our prosperity would continue to spiral upward. We never gave much thought to or questioned the roots of our prosperity. Many believe we have grown up in a very selfish society-me first, never mind the other person. We did not look at the world situation, consequently our impending vulnerability. This is where we are affected by outside forces. Canada is a trading nation and is affected by the ups and downs of the world economy.
For some time a few Canadians, the poor, the aged, the helpless, the weak, paid the price of these inflationary demands. Today only a few groups can pursue their expectations, the powerful, the protected, the privileged. It is the many who pay the cost in unemployment, in bankruptcy, in loss of opportunity. Certainly the expectations of the over one million unemployed have been shattered. These are the people who are hurt and whom we must help. This is where people in the federal service can share what they have. They can share their job security with those who are less fortunate. While there has been some criticism from some members of the federal public service arguing against being singled out, I suggest that those employed in the federal public service can be the heroes of the day by accepting the idea of reduced compensation to help in this fight against inflation. This does not mean that all the other benefits enjoyed by members of the public federal service will be done away with.
This afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) suggested that federal public servants would see a reduction in their benefits. That is absolutely incorrect. It is
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
wrong. No federal public servant will lose his job because of this program, no one will see a reduction in benefits.
The hon. member for Vancouver East was quite critical of the minister responsible for the status of women. She said the minister was all talk and no action, and she expressed concern about what this bill was doing to female workers across the country. She was right about the talk as far as that minister is concerned. No other member of this House does as much as that minister in promoting the cause of trying to help women in the work force across this country. Women's rights across this country are upheld by the minister responsible for that department.
The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) expressed concern about the future of equal employment opportunity programs and affirmative action programs in the federal public service. It is the intention of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) to continue with the development of affirmative action programs in three government departments and to pursue their introduction in other departments. The introduction of affirmative action programs is not related to collective agreements or compensation plans and consequently will not be affected by Bill C-124. We must make sure that is on the public record.
We know too that many times the federal civil service is criticized for what some term a lack of compassion and caring for those with whom they deal in the private sector. But by taking the lead in lowering expectations as to wage increases, the federal civil service will indeed be showing that they do have the good of their fellow citizens and the country as a whole at heart.
Some people and some members of the House have irresponsibly suggested that some members of the public service and the government took advantage to the situation by settling wage negotiations in the public sector prior to the June 28 budget. For example, the hon. member of the New Democratic Party for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) indicated the other day that it was reprehensible that the government should have approved a 10 per cent wage increase for lawyers in the Department of Justice just hours before the June 28 budget. I would like to advise hon. members that the Department of Justice lawyers are excluded from the collective bargaining process. Earlier this year, the lawyers employed in other government departments and agencies negotiated an 11 per cent wage increase for 1982 with the government through the collective bargaining process. The government approved the wage increases for the Justice lawyers in order to treat them in the same way as the bargaining unit lawyers. Both groups of lawyers will receive and will be limited to an increase of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent increase in 1984.
As I earlier mentioned, Mr. Speaker, members of the federal civil service can be the heroes of the day in this program. This is a fight against inflation and members of the federal civil service are the front-runners in this battle. But having said

July 13, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
this, we know too, that the federal civil service cannot win this fight alone. We all have to become involved. We all have a stake in the outcome. We all must share in the effort, each according to his own ability. I believe that Canadians are willing to make sacrifices so that others can be helped. It was refreshing to read in a letter to the editor of the Ottawa Citizen on July 8, a letter from a federal public servant and a member of the Public Service Alliance of Canada who said:
As a federal public servant and a member of the Public Service Alliance of Canada I wish to dissociate myself from the almost hysterical response of Alliance leaders, other public service unions and superannuates groups of public service salaries and pensions. 1 thank God for both the job security I enjoy and the fact I am not suffering a reduction in my salary, (many Canadians would be so lucky). My family and I will adjust to a salary increase marginally lower than the expected cost-of-living increase when the time comes.
In another letter which appeared in the same July 8 edition of the Ottawa Citizen there is this:
May I also reluctantly endorse the reduction in government spending, including my own wages. The measures being taken by the all-too-many private firms with money problems are certainly by necessity more severe.
These are letters to the editor which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen from two federal public servants.
Let me read from another news item in the July 3 edition of the Ottawa Citizen comments from retired public servants who are ready to sacrifice to help the economy, comments such as, "Annual increases unless they will buy more are useless. I agree with MacEachen and his 6 per cent and am happy to bear my share." That is from a retired federal civil servant.
Another believes cutbacks:
-might set an example for private industry. But, by the same token, anyone who is suffering should get special consideration.
Another retiree said:
If it will help, then I'll reduce my living standard.
And so it goes, Mr. Speaker. I do believe that Canadians will accept these sacrifices so that others can be helped.
What about the private sector, the provinces, the municipalities? Before the budget of June 28 there were many groups demanding action by the federal government to cure our economic ills. Many of those same groups obviously do not like the action taken by the Minister of Finance. The trouble is that those sectors of our society have conflicting interests. For example, some union leaders want interest rates and inflation to come down but they will not agree to limit their inflationbuilding wage demands. Businesses want wage controls but not price controls. Provinces still demand more money from the federal government. Individuals want tax cuts but still demand more services. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the country can evade the truth for only a short time. There must be a willingness on all our parts to share and share alike. There must be willingness on the part of the provinces and municipal governments, private business and the rank and file of the labour movement to lower financial expectations.
Here I might mention that members of the council of the city of London, the area which I represent, last week voted to reduce their salaries to increases of 6 and 5 per cent. I believe also that members of the council of the city of Kitchener have done likewise. I am sure there will be other municipalities
across this great country of ours following the same suit. Some have said that the dollar figures involved do not really amount to much. That is it not that important. On the other hand I think it is the action taken by members of the London city council that is important. I congratulate them for following the federal government's stand in this matter of a 6 per cent and 5 per cent wage increase.
On the other hand, I was rather dismayed to learn through an editorial which appeared in the London Free Press, the newspaper in that city, that secondary school teachers in London, or at least their leadership, are demanding far more than the federal anti-inflation wage guideline in their current bargaining with the London Board of Education. The editorial says that elementary school teachers as opposed to the secondary school teachers in London recently settled for a 12.5 per cent increase, which is still more than double the 6 per cent and 5 per cent suggestion. The editorial asks the question: "Where is restraint in teacher bargaining?" It suggests that negotiators for the secondary school teachers take a second look at what they are demanding in this matter of salary increases.
So we can see, of course, that there is much to be done in this country of ours, in our own local areas, of course, in trying to influence members of various sections of society who have a specific interest at heart, whether in contract negotiations or just wishing to try to contribute to this over-all fight to wrestle inflation down so that we can help those who are sorely in need not only today but, more important, those in need in the future.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I emphasize that we must all be in this battle against inflation, for we all have contributed to the economic problem of the day. Some people continue to say that rising wages and salaries have nothing to do with inflation, that it is a matter of prices which have fuelled inflation. I believe that an hon. member of the New Democratic Party, the previous speaker, referred to this. But when the cost of producing goods and services, of which wages and salaries are a major factor, rise faster than our production, they do contribute to rising prices. In the July 10 Toronto Star David Crane wrote:
In spite of sizeable pay increases over the past three or four years, few Canadians feel that they are much better off. That's not surprising. By and large, pay increases have simply led to more price increases and a more inflationary environment that has wiped out the pay gains.
The missing ingredient today is productivity, our best measure of economic progress.
He went on to say:
Education, job training, innovation, good management, research and development, sizeable investment in new machinery and equipment, government policies that encourage efficiency and the shift of resources from dying industries to growth industries all contribute to good productivity growth. And it is in these areas that Canada is lagging behind its industrial world partners.
Yet here is the important point: Pay increases can only have real value when they are matched by productivity increases. If an employer grants a wage increase and has productivity growth, then he does not have to increase the price
July 13, 1982

of his product to pay for the wage increase. But if he grants a wage increase and has no productivity growth, then he must either increase his prices or accept lower or zero profits, which means the eventual collapse of his business.
But again, we cannot put all the blame for rising prices and thus increasing inflation on wage and salary increases. Governments at all levels, business and labour, individuals and almost all of us have contributed in some degree to the economic problems of the day. And it has usually been out of selfinterest. Because of Bill C-124, limiting wage increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in the federal public service sector, there are some hopeful signs that other sectors are listening as well. The meetings which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have had with provincial leaders and with business and labour leaders, at least at first glance, give some hope for the future. For example, an article in The Globe and Mail of July 9 says:
The federal government received pledges of support yesterday from 39 senior Canadian business leaders for its goal that private-sector wage increases be voluntarily limited to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984.
I will get to the reaction of labour leaders in just a few minutes.

I am sure my friends in the New Democratic Party will not agree with the following quotations, but I must use them because they represent the view of business organizations across the country. If we did not have business organizations,

Sam Hughes, the president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, has indicated that he intends to use his influence to urge his provincial counterparts, the chambers across the country, to get into this 6 per cent solution so that we can all be in this battle together. If we listened to them, the deficit would be even higher. We would be far deeper into the hole than we are now because all we hear from them is spend, spend, spend and do this and do that-

I know what is fact. That is why I say that all we get from hon. members opposite are cries of spend, spend, spend.
