speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we see the clock tonight and when we resume tomorrow there are a few things that I should like to put on the record with regard to Bill C-124. This wage control package is a key element in the government's anti-inflation strategy, even though everyone knows that wages have been falling behind inflation for the last five or six years, and so tonight I should like to examine the subject in the total economic context.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has made it clear on a number of occasions that the public sector is to be made an example and an instrument by which wages in the private sector will be brought into this 6 and 5 per cent world which the government intends for the Canadian people.
In my riding, workers at the CN shops in Transcona will be affected by the bill, as will workers in Montreal, in Point St. Charles, in Moncton and throughout the system all across the country. It is particularly irritating to me, and it is an example of the continuing injustice done to railway workers in this country, that the people in Transcona have been told that they will be laid off for eight to ten weeks more than the normal summer lay-off-and even that was extended for a few more weeks-and then on top of that they are now told that their collective bargaining achievements for 1983 will not be respected, but instead broken through the legislative instrument of Bill C-124. The increase of 9 per cent which was scheduled for 1983 will be reduced to 5 per cent.
Apart from the obvious injustice of workers in CP shops making more than workers in CN shops by January 1983, CP Rail will be required to pay out more in wages than will the CNR. Thus, if the government does not withdraw this bill, there will be a test of its theory of economic competitiveness. If this theory is correct, the profitability of CN will soar in comparison with that of CP because CN will not have to pay its workers as high wages. According to the government, that is what affects the profitability of Canadian corporations. So we will wait with bated breath to see if that will be the case.
On a national level we are dealing with an accumulation of years and years of Liberal policies. The chickens are coming home to roost now that the United States' domination of the world economy is not what it used to be. Canada has been tied
July 13, 1982

to that economy for decades. The Liberals, with Conservative approval, openly sought the integration of the Canadian economy with the United States economy. Now we are shamefully dependent on the United States economy and on investment decisions made in that country and also in the head offices of non-American multinational corporations. Many years ago when the CCF and subsequently the NDP complained that this was not a good thing, they were regarded as the party poopers in Canada. People claimed that foreign investment was creating jobs, that there was growth, and an increase in consumer goods and services. And all that was true as long as the economy we were tied to was the dominant world economy. In a way, we regret that we were right and that the things we said about the price we might some day have to pay for this dependence on the American economy have come to pass.
I should like to share some of my views with the House on why we are in this position now. What has been going on in this country, is a strike by capital. Some would credit that to the abhorrence the private sector had for the National Energy Program. God only knows why because it was the most milquetoast Canadianization program you could imagine. But that is the extent of the pettiness and dominance of the international investment community that such a paltry move on the part of the Liberal government could cause them to take such a bruising in terms of international confidence.
There has been a capital strike going on in this country, not just since the NEP but accumulating over the years. What we have now is a Liberal government which has capitulated to the strikers. It is always amusing to me to see the criticism workers receive from the community at large when they say that unless they get a certain return on their labour, they are going to hold out until they do. Yet when the investment community in this country does that, it is called good business, initiative. It is called looking for more incentives. But when the working people of Canada do exactly the same thing, to all intents and purposes they are reviled and called upon to sacrifice and cooperate.
There are a number of things going on, Mr. Speaker. As I said before, for some time now the Americans have been suffering from a reduction in the predominance of American-controlled corporations in the global economy. Americans themselves have been the object of investment decisions by multinational corporations based in other countries. What is happening, it seems to me, is that President Reagan is saying, through his high interest rate policy, support of the American dollar and various other hidden protectionist measures, that they are going to re-establish the American economy as the predominant force in the western world. If that means putting the economy of all their allies and other industrialized countries on the block, so be it. Indeed, even if it means the sacrifice of farmers, small-business men or even larger corporations within the American context, then that is the price they are prepared to pay in order to re-establish that dominance.

However, another thing that is going on, Mr. Speaker, is that in the final analysis the Americans will not be able to reestablish their predominance over the global economy in the way they hope to because there is a restructuring of that economy going on which very few of us, including myself, can comprehend at this moment. What the American policy adds up to can be summed up in this way: "If there is a global restructuring going on", says President Reagan, "we are going to be the last to go down. We are going to be the last to have to face up to those North-South realities, those global realities, or face up to the need for a new economic order. We are going to be the last to face up to the need for new international cooperation". And nothing can provide more concrete evidence of that than the recent decision by the Americans not to sign the international Law of the Sea Treaty. They are saying, "No international co-operation for us; we are going to hold out and reign supreme."
I was interested, Mr. Speaker, in the comments of the hon. member for London West (Mr. Burghardt). I believe he said that we are pricing ourselves out of business. That is a very interesting argument and I want to go into it. It is an incorrect argument, but it has an element of truth in it. It is not something we did ourselves, as the hon. member tried to say in his speech. The fact of the matter is that this analysis of why we are not competitive on foreign markets, if indeed that is the case-and it is the case to some extent-does not ask the question: how are we supposed to compete with slavery? How are we supposed to compete with children working 12-hour days, seven days a week in South Korea in export plants set up by multinationals? How are we supposed to compete with the decisions made by the multinationals to invest in Third World countries which do not have labour laws, child protection laws, or environmental laws? Is that what the Liberals want us to compete with? There is only one way to compete with that, Mr. Speaker, and that is to become the kind of country those countries are. And that is what we in this party are not prepared to see Canada become in order to remain competitive.

That is what you are talking about, my friend, whether you realize it or not. All this rhetoric about pricing ourselves out of business and staying competitive in international markets is nonsense. We are talking about the difficult position-I quite agree-that the western industrialized economies have been put in by the decisions of a handful of very powerful global corporations to locate the manufacturing and assembly end of their businesses elsewhere.
The hon. member asks: if we do not compete, what is our future? I take that as a sad admission that what I am talking about is on the right track. What we can do, Mr. Speaker, is try to tell our people what is really going on. It will not be easy, but we have to begin here at home to get some independence from that system. It will take a long time, but we have to work in international circles for the kind of economic order in which the people of South Korea and the people of Guatemala

THE PRESS-PAYMENT OF GOVERNMENT ACCOUNT TO ETHNIC NEWSPAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 8 I spoke in this House about the Liberal government's increasing attacks on fundamental freedoms. In particular, I warned that attacks on freedom of information are designed to enlarge Liberal power at the expense of our freedoms. For example, the Kent commission is a blatant attempt to control the press. Another attempt to control the press is through huge government purchases of advertising space. The Liberal propaganda machine, running flat out to brainwash Canadians with massive amounts of taxpayers' money, to be exact $500 million, will stop at nothing to influence the media. If you do not play the Liberals' dirty game you do not get the advertising.
1 have in my hand a letter from Ira Kissin, editor of the Toronto Jewish Press, an independent newspaper in Toronto. Mr. Kissin complains of discrimination against his newspaper when he did not receive certain government advertising. He gives examples of dubious practices of paying commissions to Liberal "brokers". He has recoiled from the slimy touch of the
Canadian Media Corporation, yet another of those shadowy bodies set up to distribute Liberal propaganda and to carry on the government campaigns of discrimination, restriction and influence peddling.
Why does this government discriminate against the ethnic communities in this country? Why does it continually brand as racism any attempt by ethnic communities to be treated fairly and equally? When the government accuses them of racism it is itself racist. I brought this kind of conduct to the attention of the House in a question to the Minister of State for Multicul-turalism (Mr. Fleming). I repeated it on June 8. With typical disregard for the feelings of ethnic communities the minister's parliamentary secretary brushed off the insult to ethnic communities. He thinks I put too much pepper in my pirogis. I would like to put some pepper on his tail to make him do his job.
The attitude of this minister and his parliamentary secretary are typical of the Liberals. Ethnic peoples are taken for granted. The Liberals look on them as second-class citizens. They say there are two founding peoples and the rest are nowhere. The Official Languages Act has been extended to increase discrimination. The Liberals discriminate in favour of the so-called founding peoples in arranging job quotas in the public service. They designate more and more jobs in favour of these people. They claim they are correcting what they call "imbalances" by "affirmative action".
Affirmative action is clearly a program of discrimination. The Liberals say they have to discriminate to correct injustice. What they really do is create injustice.
Canadians should ask what is the Charter of Rights when the government openly practises discrimination, blatantly twists and restricts information and flagrantly ignores Parliament, the people's instrument of democracy.
I say that we are all Canadians and we should all be equal, whether we are Polish, French, Indian, Chinese, German, English, Ukrainian, Jewish, Italian, or whatever our racial extraction; whether we eat pirogis or pasta; whether we have funny names or speak with strange accents. What sort of equality is there when the second largest racial group in Toronto is Italian but not part of the affirmative action programs?
As a Member of Parliament, I speak for all Canadians, not just for the founding peoples, and as a true Canadian I ask for equality for all, not like those people over there, superiority for those who provide my electoral base. I recognize one Canada in which all are equal, truly equal; a Canada in which we should all be free, truly free, free from creeping government run by dishonourable men.
I look at the perverted ideology of the Kent commission and I listen to the insults of the Minister of State for Multicultur-alism. I hear the smart aleck evasions of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his corrupt cohorts; I weep for my country, brought low, robbed, defiled by men without honour, without
July 13, 1982

dignity, without integrity. They call themselves Liberals but they are vampires and leeches, sucking the blood and draining the vitality of this country, clinging to power with the grace of the serpent and besmirching authority with the integrity of thieves.
Like many Canadians I feel the spreading plague ot totalitarianism in this country. I see it in the face of our Prime Minister. I see the terrible blight caused by the sheer incompetence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), a man- and I use the term loosely-who tried hard to outdo his Prime Minister in his contempt for Parliament and in his absence of integrity. The evidence of their crimes against the Canadian people is there in their own budget figures. The evidence of their character, of their utter lack of concern for Canada, is in their holding on to power when all the country wishes them to go. They are diseased parasites in the blood of Canada.
If I may paraphrase a former more eloquent politician, for God's sake, get out of this House! If at this late date you can pretend to be men, for God's sake go.

LABOUR CONDITIONS-HEALTH AND SAFETY OF WORKERS UNDER FEDERAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity tonight to address a few comments in the late show debate to the question which 1 put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on March 26, relating to the idea of the federal government moving ahead on health and safety legislation for workers under the federal jurisdiction by centralizing it in one agency in the Department of Labour and, by this action, improving the health and safety of all federal jurisdictional workers.
In responding to my question, the Prime Minister indicated that that was the preferred course of the federal government. However, he indicated that a number of discussions were taking place among various concerned departments of government, but that in the long run the government preferred to move in that direction. I was pleased with his response.
This has been a continuing problem as we become more conscious of health and safety issues, as problems relating to these issues have become more complicated over the years, and as greater regulations have resulted. The concept of the
Adjournment Debate
centralized agency to deal with health and safety matters has been adopted by some provinces, including the province of Ontario where it was centralized in its department of labour. During the past year the Canadian Labour Congress supported the idea of one central agency to co-ordinate all federal activities in this regard.
Last November 9 I met with representatives of the CLC, especially representatives of United Steelworkers of America from Elliot Lake who are under federal jurisdiction in the uranium mines there. We went over the CLC report which proposed the idea of a centralized agency in the federal government. For instance, they pointed out that 15 departments and agencies of the federal government are concerned with health and safety, including the Treasury Board, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Atomic Energy Control Board, Labour Canada, the Department of Transport and many others.
In the brief which was presented at that time they also urged the upgrading of Part IV of the Canada Labour Code and the establishment of basic national health protection standards. What was true in that presentation on a national basis can be seen in microcosm in health and safety legislation and in the problems of uranium miners, about which I am very familiar because of the large mines in Elliot Lake, which is in my constituency.
Originally, conventional health and safety were under provincial jurisdiction. A ruling by the Department of Justice in 1978 put the responsibility for conventional health and safety under federal jurisdiction, and gradually the federal government has been taking over full responsibility for health and safety.
The Atomic Energy Control Board sets standards for radiation. Responsibility for conventional health and safety now comes under Part IV of the Canada Labour Code, but, because of the historic situation, the Ontario occupational health and safety act has been referenced to the Canada Labour Code. Inspection is gradually being taken over by the federal government, with the federal government paying for all the costs already incurred by the province, indicating that it wants to have the federal government ultimately take it over. A study is now being carried out.
But what we are looking for is a new centralized agency within the federal government where the Canada Labour (Standards) Code will not be subject to other acts of Parliament. It should be the superior act. We should start with the health and safety of the worker, and work back from there.
There are a number of areas where there should be upgrading, for instance, concerning the right to refuse to work, unsafe conditions, and health and safety committees. Much work has already taken place with consultation between the Department of Labour and the CLC as well as groups like the United Steelworkers of America.

July 13, 1982
Adjournment Debate
I know that within some federal government departments there is some resistance to this concept of one centralized agency. 1 hope that will be overcome soon. Elopefully, the government will be able to table a bill before this session recesses, so that over the course of the summer interested groups would be able to consider and review it. Then, as we move into the new fall session of parliament, we could move right ahead, adopt it and implement the improved standards for workers under federal jurisdiction. In this way, the federal government would have a standard, a model second to none in the country, which would guarantee the health and safety of all workers under federal jurisdiction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) for saying that since the introduction of the original statutory provisions for health and safety in the Canada Labour Code in 1965, the federal government has provided outstanding leadership in the field of health and occupational safety. We have done that as the result of the hard work, conscientious effort and the proven consciences of hon. members like the one we have just heard, the hon. member for Algoma. Thanks to the pressure that he has put upon us, we have maintained our leadership and our hard work in this very important area. The government intends to respond to his concerns. We intend to ensure that all aspects of federal occupational health and safety rules and regulations provide consistent and effective protection for all workers in this country.
The hon. member has referred to our record which has come about because of his hard efforts and those of some of our outstanding ministers. Ele has referred to the need for consultation. I can assure him that consultation will continue, that we will ensure that labour, management, and the private and public sectors will all have an opportunity to consult. He has also suggested the need for expanded leadership on our part in this area, and he has given us several examples of how we could follow this suggestion. I thank him for his advice and I assure him that action will be forthcoming. I hope he will continue to provide us with the insights that are so important for these advances.

SOCIAL SECURITY-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 23, 1982, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether or not the upcoming budget would involve an increase in guaranteed income supplements and Canada pension disability pensions. This question reflected the concern of the NDP caucus for those on fixed incomes who depend on the public pension system and who are seeing their standard of living seriously eroded by inflation. At that time I might have added veterans pensions, as they are also a matter of concern to us.
At that time, the Prime Minister did not answer my question, but chose instead to evade the question by referring to an earlier question by a colleague of mine in the same question period. I now understand why. We have seen the budget of
June 28 and we now know that it involved a decrease in pensions for those who receive only the old age security portion, the universal portion, and no real increase for those receiving the guaranteed income supplement.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has been saying this will mean only a $55 sacrifice in 1983 for those receiving OAS but not GIS. Our research shows that this is a false and self-serving miscalculation. The real cost to pensioners who receive only the old age security will be closer to $300 each over the next two-year period. This will be particularly difficult for the many pensioners who, although they do not receive the income-tested GIS benefits, live at or just below the poverty line, yet they are required to make the same sacrifice as pensioners who are quite affluent.
The National Council on Welfare has estimated that over
100,000	poor and near-poor elderly Canadians will have their incomes reduced as a result of the indexation limitation of the OAS which was proposed in the budget of June 28. Furthermore, there is an additional cumulative loss which starts the year that full indexing is reinstated, if indeed it is reinstated. This loss is due to the fact that re-indexing, when it takes place, will be established on a reduced basis, thus creating a permanent shortfall in benefits into the indefinite future.
In doing what they have done to old age security pensions, the Liberals have made a significant social policy decision which should not go unnoticed. They have attacked a universal program. They have set a precedent which must not go unchallenged, a precedent which demonstrates that when the Liberals have to choose between the social programs and the interests of their big-money friends, it is the big money that wins and the pensioners who lose.
We in the New Democratic Party are not surprised. We have always maintained that the loyalty to big money is the fundamental loyalty of the Liberal Party, in spite of whatever naive delusions that certain Liberal backbenchers might maintain about that party. In spite of those fantasies, when it comes to a choice between big money and pensioners, the pensioners lose. We are not surprised, but we do regret the consequences for the elderly in Canada. They deserve better than to be used as scapegoats in a fight against inflation they have not caused for the benefit of those who have caused it.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member raised a very serious topic and then treated it badly. Let me make it very clear right now that this government does not intend to abandon any of its commitments to retired Canadians-on the contrary. As public opinion grows in reaction to the June 28 budget, it is quite clear that pensioners agree with the government's actions. We have not asked Canadians to cut back at the expense of the elderly, as my hon. friend tried to claim.
My friend referred to our big-money friends, the supposed pals of the Liberal Party. No such pals exist. Those are the
July 13, 1982

people who know how to take advantage of inflation. They want to promote inflation, to continue those kinds of sick economic policies that undermine the very health of our economy because they personally make a profit from it.
We in this party say that the pensioners, the low-income earners and the veterans are the victims of inflation. That is why we must stop inflation. We have said that 12 per cent weakens our economy, that 6 per cent makes it grow and prosper. That message must be communicated.
The hon. member quite rightly brings to us, and I applaud him for it, a very sharp reminder of our duties toward vulnerable people. Let me give an equally sharp reminder to him. If he constantly panders to people's fears, constantly assures them that the government will fail, and constantly says that 12 per cent plus will be the normal, that is what will happen. People like him have an obligation to bring a message to us, but they have an equal obligation to take a message home. They must also say to people that if they demand 12 per cent, if they demand more and more out of the shrinking pie then they will rob the pie until there is no more.
We are not going to abandon our commitments to older people. We have the $35 monthly increase in the guaranteed
Adjournment Debate
income supplement; just as we have ensured that the people getting the GIS are protected and continue to get full indexing. We have met the demands of the veterans in regard to pensions, just as we have met the demands of the lower-income families in regard to the increase in child tax credits. We are now continuing our commitment to low-income Canadians.
1 would let the hon. member know that cheap rhetoric about the big gap there is, does not wash. He weakens his own argument. He must bring his argument to us and match it with a reminder to Canadians to learn how to cut down just a wee bit, in order to fight this terrible disease, inflation. It is a disease which hurts the weakest, who are the most vulnerable. If the hon. member has a message for me, he must also have one for his fellow Canadians.
